speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians today are perplexed and confused.
On the one hand, they read in the papers that a recent United Nations study has ranked Canada as having the second highest quality of life in the world. They also know that we have the second highest per capita income. They also hear on the news that the World Economic Forum in Geneva has placed Canada fifth among the countries of the world in global competitiveness. This all sounds like good news and it is.
But in too many cases those same Canadians are discovering from their own personal experience that all is not so well.
The parent whose child dropped out of high school last week may be disappointed and knowing that 30 per cent of Canadian children drop out before completing high school-one of the highest rates in the world-is no consolation. Knowing that 62 per cent of new jobs to be created in the next 10 years will require at least a high school education would really upset them.
Which of these views is right? Are we doing well or are we in trouble?
The answer, Mr. Speaker, is that both views are right.
There is no question that over the last 124 years, Canadians together have built a strong, dynamic and prosperous country. It shows in our standard of living, our health systems, our export performance and in many other ways.
That is only one part of the story, a snapshot assessment in an evolving world.
The global environment is changing before our very eyes and our productivity, our ability to produce efficiently as a nation is just not keeping pace. It is not growing as fast as it used to and is not gaming as fast as our competitors. This is the other side of the story which shows up in its own more negative way.

This is the other side of the story, the negative side.
The young scientist just out of university is angry and frustrated that he cannot find a job. Like thousands of our young people, he is talented and has worked hard. But with only four Canadian manufacturing firms out of 100 doing any research and development, his talent and hard work may not find the outlet they deserve.

The young factory worker is worried as she sees her friends laid off and her own shifts shortened. She does not want to go on unemployment insurance but she is probably working for one of those 50 per cent-plus of Canadian manufacturers using not one of the 22 leading manufacturing technologies essential to success in the

Routine Proceedings
1990s. As their productivity falls behind, they lose orders and she and her friends lose their jobs.
The young couple about to have their first child are not quite sure why they are having trouble making ends meet on two incomes when their parents lived comfortably on one. The reason is quite simply that their companies cannot afford to pay them more because the companies' productivity will not allow them to do so.
Productivity is the heart of the issue and is essential to our prosperity. It supports our way of life, it puts food on our tables, schools and hospitals in our communities, roads across our great country and pay cheques in our pockets.

But in order to be more productive, we first have to upgrade every component of our economy. And in order to do that, we have to learn to innovate, to work smarter and faster, instead of harder and longer.

That is why we are here today. We must find a way as a nation to improve our productivity. The old ways which served us so well are no longer working. We must change the way we think, the way we work and the way we work together as a country and as a people.
To be sure, some companies are doing what needs to be done. They are ploughing back their profits into productive new investment. They are spending on research and development and introducing sophisticated new equipment. Many individuals are not only seeking but actually making new opportunities for themselves by upgrading their skills and exploring new challenges. In a word they are adapting to the changing world around them.
But too many of us are simply not changing far enough or fast enough to keep up with the global pace-setters for much longer. The underlying cause of this state of affairs is far beyond the capacity of government, any government, to turn around on its own.
The Speech from the Throne in May put on record the government's intention to invite all Canadians "to participate in fashioning a new agenda for prosperity", to tell us what we must change in order to compete and win in the world. Over the summer, the initial response of
Canadians has been clear: Take action but consult us first.
For these reasons I am pleased to inform the House that the government is today instituting a comprehensive consultation process. It will be managed by a national steering committee and designed to elicit from all sectors of Canadian society the solutions to the challenges now confronting us.

I am particularly delighted to announce that two very distinguished Canadians, Mr. David Robert McCamus and Mme Marie-Josee Drouin, have agreed to act as co-chairpersons of the Steering Committee in its tasks of managing the public consultations and developing a plan of action.
The Steering Group will be made up of representatives from the business, academic, labour and scientific communities, as well as leading economic and social organizations.

The group will consult communities across the country as well as provincial governments and other national organizations. In addition, it will benefit from specific industry discussions conducted by cabinet ministers.
Mr. Speaker, I am also pleased to table a discussion paper entitled Prosperity Through Competitiveness. This, together with a companion paper that my colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration will be tabling in a few minutes, will serve as a focus for these consultations.
Together, the papers identify areas in which we must improve so that we can compete effectively, efficiently and profitably. Each area-learning, science and technology, investment, domestic markets and trade-is important. None of the components of the prosperity initiative is revolutionary. But they are the nuts and bolts of the country's economy.
Because time is of the essence, we have asked the steering group to complete its consultations by mid next year and to produce its final action plan by the end of next summer.
The change that is needed must not be a quick fix. The competitive challenge can only be met by systemic changes and not piecemeal changes; by sustained, not sporadic commitment to compete with the best in the world.
October 29, 1991

Canadians may have to change the way we think-all of us, from cabinet maker to cabinet minister-if we can ever hope to change the way we act. Because how we act is the real test of how productive we are going to be. We cannot sustain our standard of living unless we strengthen our ability to compete.
Whatever plan of action results from this process we are launching today, it will be important that as a country we strike while the iron is hot. We must act on our plan quickly and collectively while we are still able to do so from a position of relative strength and prosperity, with the capacity to generate wealth to support the changes that are needed.
It is time for us to maximize our use of something we have in abundance, our ingenuity. Millions of Canadians can still remember when Canadians had the best hockey teams in the world. Year in and year out, Canadians took for granted that their teams would come home with lopsided victories. Then, in the 1960s, someone from
11,000	kilometres away figured out how to beat us. They changed the way our game was played. They outskated, outshot and outchecked us. We were still playing good hockey, but they were playing better. They beat us and kept beating us until we learned how to innovate, how to adapt, how to upgrade and how to outsmart them. Now we are winning again because we have changed. We are winning again, but not all the time because competition is tougher today than it was in the 1960s.
We have built our team back to being among the best and can remain among the best if we continue to innovate and improve.

As a country, we are like our hockey team. We spent our first one hundred years living off our resources, and we beat the competition easily. For the next twenty years, we lived off our credit and found we were slipping. Now we have to demonstrate that we can recover our position off the ice as well as on it.

Our history tells us that we can come back. Individuals and companies are showing every day that we can do it by innovating and upgrading. Now we have to do the same as a country. Whenever we put our minds to a problem, we have licked it. I said this morning that we have
Routine Proceedings
something to be concerned about, and we have. However, I am reassured by the knowledge that when Canadians roll up their sleeves, the job gets done. I know we can do it.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with attention to the minister's introduction of his long-delayed consultation paper Prosperity through Competitiveness. That paper was promised to the people of Canada last May in the Speech from the Throne. Here we are more than six months later finally getting a paper.
The problem with the paper is not merely that it has been so long delayed and has not fulfilled the promise made by the government so many months ago, but rather that the paper is lacking in substance. The problem is that this paper offers Canadians no solutions, no directions and no proposals about how we resolve our serious problems of international competitiveness in Canada.
The minister knows perfectly well that after all these months of preparation, to bring forward such a paper is really an admission on the part of the government of its own failure to devise, develop and identify solutions to the problems which have confronted Canadians throughout this government's mandate. I do not speak only of the last three years or two years. I am speaking of the time since 1984 when this government first came to office.
This government at that time inherited a burgeoning economy left by the previous government. Look at the statistics. Anyone will be able to identify for themselves quite readily that in 1984 growth was well in place and benefiting all Canadians. What have we today after its seven or eight years in office? We have a paper from this government that says: "We don't know what to do. We are now going to go out on the road for a year's consultation with Canadians about what they think should be done". The government offers a paper which under various headings such as learning, innovation, financing, and domestic market regulation asks merely vague questions. Vague is a kind word. The questions are barely formulated, and the answers are certainly not offered. There are no options provided. There is not even any indication that after seven years this government has any idea of what to do about Canada's international competitiveness.

Routine Proceedings
Let me say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the real failure of this government in its economic policies over the past seven years is not what it has done, it is what it has failed to do.
You know, Mr. Speaker, as well as I do that the macroeconomic or what the economists would call a macroeconomic environment is essential if Canada is going to compete effectively abroad. But what have we got in Canada? We have not had the government providing the leadership or offering the macroeconomic circumstances which can enable Canadians to compete effectively abroad.
We have high interest rates and a continuing high debt. The debt is at least as high as it was last year and with every indication it will continue at a very high level next year. We have a high Canadian dollar resulting from this government's failure to address its spending priorities and its failure to achieve lower interest rates so as to enable Canadians to compete effectively abroad.
This government has failed on the macro level and now it turns to what we might call the micro level which deals with specific instances of where Canadians know perfectly well we must take action. We must take action on training and retraining. We must take action on how we direct our savings toward productive investment. We must take action on innovation within our economy and the vital role to be played by science, technology, research and development. What do we get instead? We get a series of questions. We know the questions. All Canadians know the questions. We have known these questions for six and seven years.
What about the creation within Canada of a true economic union within our own country? This is an essential basis for our further progress in international competition.
But only now in its constitutional proposals has the government come forward with a few vague ideas. It may be vague on the one side, and highly convoluted in some detail on the other, about what it is going to do to create true economic union within our country.
The foundations are lacking in this paper to give Canadians any indication of how we might best proceed. The leadership is lacking. Let me turn for a moment to
international trade. The paper ends with a couple of vague questions. Should we trade more? That is the sort of question posed.
I think most Canadians would probably agree, yes, we should trade more. So the government then asks the question: "How do we do it?"
Clearly the government has no clear idea itself of how to do it. The government is right when it says: "Maybe we spent a little too much time on continentalism. Maybe we spent a little too much time on the free trade agreement and now on an agreement with Mexico". This, by any stretch of the imagination, can hardly be given Canadian priority. It said "Maybe we spent too much time on these issues and maybe we should be looking at Asia and the new Europe of 1992".
It has taken seven years for the government to think that one through. It does not even offer that as a nostrum. It simply says: "What do you think, Canada? Should we do this? Should we look at this?"
The real failure of this government, as I said, is what it has not done over the past seven years. It has failed to create an economic environment of spending restraint, taxation restraint and of creating lower interest rates and a stable dollar so that Canadian exporters can progress and expand at home and abroad in a way that creates the jobs that Canadians so obviously need. We do not have any comprehensive system of adjustment programs. The government now, at this late date, is saying that maybe we should have some comprehensive adjustment programs.
The decision on the free trade agreement was taken three or four years ago.
We are only now saying to ourselves: "Maybe we should have a little more training and retraining". What has this government really done about removing the trade barriers within our own country?
Canadians have known. They are not stupid people. They have known that those barriers should come down. They were in the constitutional proposals of the previous government, and it was due to the failure of the provinces to recognize their importance that we did not make any progress at that time. Now seven and eight years later we are saying: "Oh well, maybe we should make a little progress there".

"Let us look beyond the continent of North America", it says. We have been telling the government for years that it should be looking beyond the continent of North America. Its obsession with continentalism has led it to a blindness to the opportunities outside North America for Canadian exporters and Canadian investors.
Finally, it is the failure of this government to link its social policies and economic policies in an effective manner so as to ensure that the undeniable costs of the emerging global economy are spread equitably among our people, as are the benefits, when we come to achieve the real gains from the emerging global economy of which I have spoken.
This paper fails in that it offers Canadians only a series of vague questions and one more year of discussion before we can possibly hope to see any solutions emerging. My colleague from Newfoundland has a word or two to add. I would suggest that I now turn this over to him.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, last week I met with groups of workers in Windsor who have lost their jobs in the last 18 months.
There were three different groups totalling perhaps 225 people all out of work from plant shutdowns, all taking retraining of various sorts to try to get back into the work force. I want to quote from one of those workers.
"I came to this country 28 years ago. I worked 11 years at Bendix company. It closed down in 1981. I lost those eleven years of my life. I got a job at Windsor Bumper and it closed too. I came here for a better future, but now I am in the same position I was 28 years ago, with no job".
"What kind of future can I give my kids if this government does not change and give them a better future?" That is what this debate is about. It concerns people: men and women who have lost their jobs and their children who share that cost.
The government has brought forth more paper, all sorts of paper, more fancy phrases and more plans for consultation. Of course, we are glad to see the government taking seriously some of the things that it has so
Routine Proceedings
long neglected, like better training and more research and development.
Let us not permit the pretence to pass. This government is responsible for those workers whose plants have been closed; extreme interest rates, 6 per cent above the U.S. level, a value of the dollar up 25 per cent since 1987, a trade deal with the United States that was so unfair it has cost at least 250,000 permanent jobs. It is responsible for tax breaks to the rich and the GST for the rest of Canadians. All this has devastated our economy.
Yes, Canadians are perplexed and confused.
Unemployment is increasing. More and more people have to swallow their pride and survive the best they can on meagre welfare payments, and we have the GST.
In Quebec, for instance, medicare is on the way to being privatized because the government is cutting transfer payments to the provinces, and so on.
Until now, the Tory government blamed the deficit for the additional tax burden. I am referring to the tax burden on Canadians who pay their taxes, not the corporations that get off scot-free with their expense accounts for restaurants and all kinds of tax deductions.
Now that people are increasingly perplexed, because they are beginning to understand that all their problems are due to the government's incompetence, the Tories turn around and serve up a new slogan: Competitiveness. They want to cover up their failures with nice speeches.

Remember, I ask people across this country, even the business oriented Conference Board of Canada has labelled this the made-in-Canada recession, made by the ministers and the government sitting across from us in this House of Commons.
What we have here are not the prosperity papers. These are the propaganda papers. They are meant to divert Canadians from the real issues. They are meant to say that the basic Tory thrust is just fine; here are the restricted issue areas where we all have to concentrate and work together.

October 29, 1991
Routine Proceedings
I have to ask how this minister can get up and call for Canadians to co-operate when this same minister has kicked those Canadians in the teeth for the last seven years with his policies.
New Democrats believe in business-labour co-operation but aimed at full employment which these papers never mentioned. New Democrats believe the tax system needs reviewing to make it fairer, like cutting out loopholes for the rich, cutting out benefits for the powerful and doing away with the job destroying GST.
New Democrats want better training in this country but not at the expense of a much harsher UIC system. Just throwing workers on to welfare, that is what the Conservatives have given us. New Democrats want more consultation but on the real questions of the GST; the trade deal, whether it should extend to Mexico; the value of the dollar; interest rate policies; whether inflation should be our ultimate concern when 1.4 million Canadians are unemployed.
I am pleased to announce the first five New Democrat consultations which will take place in Hamilton, Guelph, London, Kingston and Sarnia between November 21 and December 17 of this year.
We can build the economy that we want and need for our people, but first we have to get rid of this government which we do not want. That means recognizing these propaganda papers as the first shot in the Conservative re-election campaign. As the $20 million is spent on this propaganda push, this diversion from the real issues, let every taxpayer recognize that their money is paying for this Tory pre-election campaign.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table today, in both official languages, a discussion paper supporting the government's Prosperity initiative and entitled "Learning Well-Living Well".
Parliament's most important function in a democratic society like ours, even before resolving conflicting views or seeking consensus, is first to inform. To inform
ourselves, yes, and also to inform Canadians. When the objective is to inform Canadians of a threat to the continued prosperity, and ultimately the unity, of the nation-even if the message is unsettling and unwelcome at first to most-then this has to be Parliament's most important calling, Mr. Speaker, and its finest hour. This, Mr. Speaker, is what we are doing today-informing the Canadian people of an intolerable situation.
The government is putting forward to this House and to all Canadians a well-reasoned and thoughtful statement on a major international challenge that cannot be ignored. This is the competitive threat to the long-term security and prosperity of all Canadians.
The only way for Canadians to meet this threat is to develop our most valuable national asset: people. It is not Canada's natural resources but our human resources-our brain power-that count. It is ideas, knowledge, and skills that will be our winning ticket.
Our major international competitors are doing a better job than we are on this score, Mr. Speaker. The gap between our performance and theirs is widening. It will widen even further, unless we are determined to stop it and to take effective action now. We have one of the highest high-school dropout rates in the world: 30 per cent to Japan's 2 per cent. We face a critical shortage of scientists and engineers: Japan graduates nearly nine times as many as we do. People will say, "Japan again!"
Even Mexico, a developing country, graduates four times as many. Of course, these countries have a much bigger poopulation than Canada, Mr. Speaker, but I am talking on a per capita basis. More statistics? We are ranked 11th in the responsiveness of our school system to meet the demands of global competition. We rank 20th out of 24 OECD member countries in the effectiveness of our training programs.
Canadian companies spend proportionately only half of what American companies spend on training, one fifth of what the Japanese spend and only one eighth of what the Germans spend. Less than 50 per cent of adult Canadians have completed high school-that is, 12 years of schooling. Yet we know that 63 per cent of all jobs in the coming decade will require at least a high school certificate and 40 per cent will require at least 16 years of schooling.
October 29, 1991

Tragically, three out of ten adult Canadians cannot read properly and four out of ten cannot do simple arithmetic. Canada has one of the worst levels of literacy and numeracy among our competitors.

The solution to this widening gap lies in the minds and actions of individual Canadians. Canadians must want to value far more learning through life, that is develop a learning and training culture. This means that Canadian firms, especially small and medium sized ones, would quadruple and more the time and resources devoted to training and create a training culture within their firms. Life-long learning can become as important to us as it is to our international competitors: a life passion for gaining new knowledge and skills to compete, yes, but also to grow.
Right now as a people we do not have this commitment. This is the unfortunate reality. This is the central challenge every Canadian should see and confront.

If we do not, Mr. Speaker, in the coming years, we will lose high-skill, high-wage jobs, the security of all our jobs, and face an inevitable decline in our living standard. The threat will not diminish, but only grow!
This is a call to Canadians first and foremost to perceive fully the nature of the challenge-to dialogue and learn anew, and then in partnership, devise a response to this crisis. Let us be crystal-clear about it: the federal government has a responsibility to stimulate a national dialogue on Canada's economic future. For those who are concerned that the federal government will use this as a pretext to intrude on provincial jurisdiction, I want to say emphatically that this is not the case, Mr. Speaker. It would not be permitted by the Constitution, and in any case, it would make no sense. No one should fear that the people of Canada, in every province and every region, become better informed and talk seriously among themselves.
That is what we propose and that is what Canadians should expect of their federal government. If the federal government, knowing the facts, failed to inform Canadians, it would be a terrible abdication of ledership.
Routine Proceedings
Surely we are not so insecure and lacking in self-assurance to be concerned with the national government informing Canadians and encouraging them to talk seriously among themselves.
The Japanese or Germans or Italians are not going to put out press releases or prepare serious discussion papers for Canadians to alert us to our lower levels of performance.

They and other nations will send their message by cancelling contracts.

Canadian firms will get the pink slip when they submit their bids or lose the opportunity to bid at all. The door to the international marketplace will be slammed in our face. Then the message to Canadians will have arrived a bit too late. We are putting learning at the front of the national agenda and to fail to do so knowing what we know would be totally irresponsible.
We should all celebrate that the results of this dialogue that we are starting today will be that Canadians will become more empowered. Individuals and all institutions in Canada, in partnership with each other and government, will find the answers. We want and welcome a public debate on Canada's economic future. Only then can we pave the way for a consensus to be forged on how to compete and to win against the best in the world.
Today in Canada until the throne speech put forward the challenge on learning and made learning part of the national agenda and consciousness, few Canadians placed the priority where it belongs. Now Canadians have a basis to consider launching themselves on a new journey. The rewards for each will be great if we put ourselves and our children firmly and for all time on this new path. Prosperity and personal growth will be the outcome as we confidently take on the world.
Business as usual is not an option. To fail to respond to this challenge ensures our economic decline. We would be left behind as other nations redouble their efforts to outperform and outcompete us.
We will rob our lives and our nation of the enormous potential that is ours.

October 29, 1991
Routine Proceedings

The Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney, stated forcefully at the First Ministers' Conference in 1989 that we must launch a collective study of our education system, its relationship to Canadian competitiveness and its relevance to the international challenges of the year 2000.
His expression of leadership was positively received by all provincial premiers not as an attempt by the federal government to intrude into provincial jurisdiction but as a recognition that this truly was an issue of interest and importance to all Canadians.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that we can all have the self-assurance and confidence to consider this paper and input from any other source objectively and start a national dialogue.
All hon. members and all Canadians should consider this challenge very carefully.

In doing so every member of this House has the opportunity, if not the duty, to do the right and responsible thing, to boldly assert leadership and help Canadians realize their full potential and secure their prosperity into the 21st century.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suspect that the emotion I feel right now is not different from that of other Canadians who have tuned into this speech and presentation by two ministers, one on prosperity, one on the need for training, with a sense of hope.
I got up this morning at 7 a.m. and came down to Parliament Hill for an eight o'clock briefing behind closed doors to be given some background information as the opposition employment critic with a sense of hope. I come from a riding that suffers tragically high unemployment, among the highest in the country. I come from a constituency where every family has some members, and in many cases a majority of members, who have left not only home but their province in desperate search for work. I come from a part of the country where we need more training. We need to give people the skills that are required to be competitive in the national economy and in the increasing global economy.
All I feel having heard the speech of the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Employment is that I have been the victim of a cruel hoax.
The Government of Canada has not laid before the people of Canada today propositions, proposals, dealing with plans to enhance our prosperity or plans to give Canadians the skills they need, the tools they need to contribute. No, there is nothing specific. It has given us a report that tells us there is a crisis. After seven years of government, almost eight years, these ministers stand up today and with a sense of pride and with great alarm, as if they discovered it just yesterday, they ask us, did we know after nearly eight years of government, do we Canadians know.
They want us to know. They want us to be alarmed because they just found out their alarm. At what? That we have one of the highest high school drop-out rates in the world after nearly eight years of this government, that we face a critical shortage of scientists and engineers after nearly eights years of this government, that we are ranked eleventh in responsiveness of our school system, that we are ranked twentieth out of twenty-four in the effectiveness of our training programs world-wide, that Canadians companies spend only one-half, 50 per cent as much as American companies on training, and that less than 50 per cent of current adults have completed high school, that only three out of ten adults in Canada read properly.
This is the report card of the government on itself after eight years. It is a report card of failure. It is an admission of failure after eight years.
What are the facts? It takes tremendous nerve and a small degree of backbone. It takes, as we say in Newfoundland, a lot of guff. As we say in Newfoundland, you bought the face of a robber's horse as it departs the scene of the crime to stand in the House and say, as this minister has just said, and I wrote it down: "We are going to put education at the front of the national agenda''. We, this government, this Mulroney administration that has been in power nearly eight years, is telling us today, October 29, 1991: "We are going to put education at the front of the national agenda".
October 29, 1991

What has this government done in the area of education? It has been in power now going on eight years, what has it done? It has reduced contributions to post-secondary education funding since 1986. Between 1986 and 1994, the formula calls for a $9.5 billion cut for education.
Today it wants us to believe that it is going to put education at the front of the national agenda. That takes nerve. There is a better word than that.
This is the government that has frozen Canada student loans at the same level they were at when it came into power in 1984. Most recently, it has introduced a 3 per cent tax applicable for the first time this year on student loans. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, the student who is wealthy, no tax; the student who is among the poorest in Canada who is required to get a loan now pays a tax on his loan. The bigger the loan, the bigger the tax.
This is the government that has the nerve to tell us today that it is putting education at the forefront of the national agenda, taxing education, taxing student loans. This is the government that applied the GST to books and to other student aids, brought in the GST and did not exempt education, but applied it. Yes, tuition fees are exempt, but books and other learning aids are not exempt.
The government has announced its large campaign to deal with functional illiteracy. What did it announce? It announced that roughly 5 million Canadians are functionally illiterate in this country. It has announced a $20 million program for five years to combat illiteracy. It just told us, in its statement, that 3 out of 10 people are functionally illiterate. The government is going to spend $4.40 per illiterate Canadian annually. It is slightly more than one penny per day per functionally illiterate Canadian.
The government has just moved education to the front of the national agenda and 1.3 pennies per day per functionally illiterate Canadian will be spent in the great campaign that this government has launched to deal with illiteracy.
This government says it is going to consult. It says that this is a real effort to consult. It wants business and labour and government working together in harmony. If we did not know better we would think today's announcement was the latest script for the Smurfs television program, it has such childlike delight in its simplicity and, might I add, phoniness.
Routine Proceedings
The minister who just spoke, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, announced on January 14, 1991 the creation of the Canadian Labour Force Development Board. Here is the minister's press release and I want to quote him: "The Canadian Labour Force Development Board will play a key role in developing a training culture and a commitment to training excellence. It will advise on national training and labour-market adjustment priorities." It goes on for several more paragraphs to talk about this board and its position at the key, at the nerve centre of training and development in Canada. Its role is to bring together all the players in the community and to advise government.
Yesterday, I spoke to one of the co-chairs of that board. He told me something I find absolutely incredible and astonishing. The co-chairman told me that they had not been consulted on the minister's discussion paper on training released today. That is what he told me. He told me further that the board would not be participating in the consultations once the paper was released. That is what the co-chairman, Gerard, told me yesterday. He told me that the board will not play any role in this consultation process.
What is the reality? I want Canadians to know the reality. The government has announced in an initiative today-mark it down, October 29,1991-that is at least a $20 million initiative. We got that in the briefing this morning that I came to. There is $2.5 million so far estimated to be spent on community-based town hall consultations, $7.5 million so far for a secretariat for this new prosperity training committee, $5 million estimated so far-listen members opposite-for advertising, for communications for this secretariat, and an undetermined amount of money to be used for giving contracts to consulting agencies to write papers for the secretariat.
Now we are up to $20 million and that is the day it was launched. It will be $25 million or $30 million or $35 million or $40 million to be spent on this so-called effort to put education at the front of the national agenda.
Let us be honest. There is not one single piece of data, there is not one fact spoken today by the minister of employment or by the minister for trade that we were not already aware of. You can find any one of 25 reports by Commons committees, by various departments of the government, by the Conference Board of Canada. I participated in a report in 1981 that looked at a lot of

Routine Proceedings
these problems emerging which have since been grandly exacerbated by this government. There is nothing new.
Is the government today in the business of trying to address the problems of prosperity or the need for prosperity? Is it really in the business of trying to address a government that has cut arbitrarily transfer funds, given no money for illiteracy, piled taxes on poor students? Is it really in the business of promoting education? Or is this government using $20 million and a third party to resurrect a dying government, led by a leader who no longer wants to be leader? Imagine, a government led by a Prime Minister who is actively flinging his resume around looking for a new job, trying to convince us now after eight years that it is serious about the mess of the economy and that it is serious about training in this country.
We on this side believe in calling it exactly what it is: this is a cruel hoax, this is a farce, this is a government at 10, 11, 12, 13 per cent in the polls-depending on which poll you believe-using taxpayers' money and a third party to try and sell a policy that has been consistently rejected by the people of Canada over the last year or two or three.
If this government had one ounce of shame, it would go out in the slightly frozen turf, dig a hole and bury its head.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I heard the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and International Trade compare Canada's competitive situation with a hockey game. It is quite evident that in so far as government leadership is concerned, our leadership consists of a number of hockey pucks.
The trifle of the discussion paper on education submitted by the Minister of Employment and Immigration is called Learning Well and Living Well. What we have heard today demonstrates that the first part of the title should have been, in respect of this government, "Learning Slow and for Canadians a Living Hell", if one pays attention to what my colleague had to say about the terrible toll of unemployment and misery that has been
imposed upon Canadians by this government through its policies. To the extent that it has any policies having to do with the economy, these have consisted of such things as the GST, a high dollar, high interest rates, and so on, which perhaps I will say something about a little later.
Only a government that did not know its way would pay a million dollars to an American Harvard professor to tell Canadians that this country is too resource dependent, that it should have more manufacturing, that it does not have enough scientists, that it does not have enough technicians, that education needs to be enhanced and reformed so that Canadians can compete.

subtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENT ENTITLED "LEARNING WELL-LIVING WELL'
speechtext: What was their first clue?

subtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENT ENTITLED "LEARNING WELL-LIVING WELL'
speechtext:
That was evidently the clue that did it. However, what one has to realize is that what we are hearing today is nothing new. It took all this time for it to penetrate into the minds of this government that we have a serious problem with respect to education and training, research and development, and science and technology.
I can recall the government convening an economic conference in 1985 and subsequent to that it has had all kinds of forums, in Halifax, Toronto, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, and Vancouver in respect to education, in respect to science and technology. It has had the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology. It has any number of specialist organizations speaking on behalf of the technology industry in this country. Every one has said the same thing. Yet for seven years this government has absolutely ignored the fact that we have fewer scientists and engineers than Japan, Germany, France and Great Britain and practically every one of the industrialized nations. Almost everyone who has looked at our situation has realized that Germany, Japan and even the United States-my God, in some respects even Mexico-outstrips us in producing trained workers.
I cannot understand how it is possible for a government to come before the Canadian people today and shock Canadians into understanding what has taken this government so long to understand and it is that it has been on the wrong track.


In fact, back when the free trade debate was going on, a great many of us pointed out that to enter into a free trade agreement such as this country did with the United States was going to confront our nation with a considerable challenge that the free trade agreement by its specifics did not allow us to meet.
In negotiating the deal, the government looked at the Canadian economy in the traditional sense that resources would somehow carry us through and we could give away all of the tools for improving Canada's manufacturing sector and improving Canada's performance. It had already become clear that we had to improve our performance in respect to value added. In fact, if we were going to enter into an agreement with the United States, we said as a party, then we should not open up the economy completely to competition from the United States unless we took the steps to correct the structural deficiencies in our economy.
I notice that as usual our Minister of Employment and Immigration talks about people in terms of national assets. He talks about human resources. I think this demonstrates the difference between the attitude of this government and my party. This is a government that speaks exclusively on behalf of those that would use what is in this country to make a profit. Everything out there, our resources and so on, are tools for making money without paying any attention to the human values and the human concerns that we think are most important.
We said that before we enter into such a free trade agreement with the United States, among other things, we should look at the capacity of our people to exercise their creativity and their capacity to innovate, to develop their skills so that they could reap the rewards of their efforts and not have someone else reap their rewards on their behalf using those people on whose behalf we speak as their resources for making profit.
If this country is going to grow and prosper it is perfectly clear that we are going to have to look upon this as an effort in which we are engaged together. I heard the Liberals talk about the failure of this government with respect to economic policy, its failure with respect to research and development policy, its failure with respect to educational leadership and so on. Just as this government cut back on transfer payments for post-secondary education, just as this government cut back on investment in research and development, just as this government has failed to provide the support for
Routine Proceedings
increasing our capacity to innovate, just as this government has in fact attacked post-secondary education, attacked research and development in so many ways, the previous government is just as much guilty as this government is in its failure because of Canada's position economically, in competition with other nations in this world, has deteriorated over the last seven years. It started deteriorating 20 years ago under a Liberal government that was just as much a failure as this government is.
We have the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and International Trade, a minister who as Minister of Finance completely ignored the pleas from this side of the House to do something about increasing investment in R and D. When this minister was Minister of Finance, he was the one that caused the Prime Minister's promise, that there would be a doubling of expenditures in research and development in this country, to be broken.
It is this Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and International Tirade, whose high valued dollar has caused almost a collapse in research and development and technology transfers in the automotive industry as testified to by reports from his own department which demonstrate that to be true, and there has been no compensation for that.
Mr. Speaker, our party is for consultation. Our party is for the participation of the people in doing something to improve the lives of Canadians, to ensure that Canada will prosper and that its citizens will have the benefit of a good livelihood based upon knowledge, training and skills.
We are outraged that this government should be suddenly shocked or pretend to be shocked by the fact that Canada faces an educational crisis and an economic crisis. This party was warned that this was happening for seven years, and before that.
We have made specific suggestions, some of which I find discussed in the government document on education, such as a grant levy system on industry to improve industry's performance and training, and a training and educational pool for youth. We have made suggestions for increasing the allotted money provided for universities and have asked for six years for a negotiated approach by the federal and provincial governments to university financing.

October 29, 1991
Routine Proceedings
We have talked for seven years about increasing the amount of money provided to the granting councils. We can stand here and list, one by one, the propositions we have advanced for improving training, improving education and for providing national leadership with respect to educational goals, all of which have been ignored.
Now the minister stands before us and says: "My God, it is the proudest moment in my life". He stood up and said what we have been saying for seven years.
I am glad that this slow learning government has caught up with the rest of the country. It has caught up with those of us who have tried to speak on behalf of this country, but it pretends that it is acting while the iron is hot.
The iron has already cooled. I hope the Canadian people, however, will put a fire under it so that this government will begin to act, not talk, not delay, not pretend to be an advocate and a participant in increasing our capacity as a country to prosper.

I believed and I still do that they are both sincere and both bargaining in good faith.
