Mr. Speaker, I too would like to make a few comments on behalf of the opposition and the Liberal Party as they relate to the negotiations and discussions of all members involved in this particular back-to-work legislation, Bill C-40.
One of the areas of major concern last night in committee was clause 7. If we look at clause 7 very
October 29, 1991

carefully it suggests to the arbitrator that the conciliation report and the recommendations in it would be used as the final arbitrator's decision if they could not come to some consensus as among Canada Post, the union and the arbitrator on what was decided during the mediation with Mr. Gold.
It was our belief as the opposition and my belief personally that this particular clause would tie the hands of the arbitrator so severely that in essence he or she could not get the job done in an effective way. Yesterday we as a party presented an amendment which we thought would rectify the issue of tying one of the arbitrator's hands behind his back. It was discussed very thoroughly for quite a length of time. As a matter of fact, we did not finish until late last night around 11.30. The clause that we referred to was to allow the arbitrator, as I said, to just take cognizance of the conclusions and recommendations set out in the report of the conciliation board submitted to the parties on August 16, 1991 and not to have to accept the recommendations forthwith.
Having said that, the minister today has submitted an amendment to us in this place. Looking at it first hand, I would say that it meets the requirements that we were looking for. The employer, the union and the arbitrator are to look at the substantial agreement and the issues that were in the substantial agreement through the mediation process, even further than that, not just through the mediation process, but the last weekend that the union and the company negotiated on their own.
It is very important for people to understand that without this amendment the arbitrator would have to look specifically at the conciliation recommendations and not at discussions that took place at the mediation process because there is no information and no report was made by the mediators. It was basically all a verbal discussion. As we learned last night, after Mr. Gold's process, all the information that was dealt with during that time was shredded. It would then become what the union believes was said versus what the company believes what was said and then the arbitrator would have difficulty coming to some sort of consensus. He would therefore have to revert back to the recommendation of the conciliator's report.
Government Orders
That conciliation report was never intended to be an arbitrator's recommendation or report. It was there as a part of the process to help people work toward a final resolution to this dispute.
I commend the minister for having the wisdom to see the difficulties that he was placing the arbitrator in. Arbitrators, as you well know, have gained a large respect in the labour movement and in our collective bargaining process because of their ability to be independent and deal with issues based on the give and take at the moment of the presentations that are made by both sides.
I want to reiterate again the opposition's sense of frustration with this whole process that we are undertaking today. We will tell you very firmly that we will not try and hold up this legislation because it is the will of the government to put it in. But we would also like to state very clearly that the legislation was unnecessary at this time. Before the minister introduced the legislation and the discussions that ensued on Friday, both parties were quite willing to continue the negotiating process. The government was frustrated with how slow things were working relative to this process and wanted to speed it up by introducing legislation that would, in its belief, force the parties to come to some sort of conclusion.
Anyone who is involved in the labour movement more than two days will tell you that the exact opposite happens when you threaten them with legislation. In most cases the company and management feel more comfortable with an arbitrator. They are quite willing to sit back and let the arbitrator rule simply because nine out of ten times, if you take a look back at the arbitrators' reports and the recommendations and the agreements that have come out of arbitration, you usually get a slant to the management side. Statistics will bear that out. It is proof that this kind of situation forces the labour movement and the unions involved to try to work out a settlement without going to arbitration. They feel that the compromises made will always be a step backward for the men and women who are involved in that particular dispute.
Once the government and the minister opposite made that decision to enter into back-to-work legislation and put it in this House, the collective bargaining that we are so familiar with ceased. It was completely done at that time.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
I want to say to the government that if that situation continues, it is going to create some significant difficulties not only for this particular dispute, but for the relationship between management and labour in the long run.
It is my view and the view of this party that is not the way things should be done. When we get our opportunity to govern this great country of ours again, we will look at things much differently than this government has as it approaches the discussion of labour/management relations.
I want to verify that by reading into the record a letter I just received this morning from an individual in Scarborough, Ontario, who wrote to me and said:
Dear Mr. Nault:
Today on the noon news I heard that talks between post office and CUPW have broken off. As a postal worker this grieves me deeply. On the same news report the minister in charge of postal affairs said if we go back out on strike, he would introduce back-to-work legislation. We, the postal workers are in a legal strike situation. Going out on strike is our only means of getting our employer, the post office, to negotiate. To remove the right to strike by legislation destroys the very essence of our Canadian collective bargaining system. If the employer never has to bargain with us in good faith, what chance have ordinary Canadian workers to maintain a decent standard of living? We have been without a contract for over two years and no end is in sight. Why cannot the parties involved reach a fair and equitable settlement?
That letter was from a postal worker by the name of Stephen Miosich.
Mr. Speaker, I want to suggest to you that it is also my personal feeling that if we take away the right to strike, we are simply suggesting that there is another mechanism in place that is more effective. If the government firmly believes that, then why does it not bring legislation forward which will suggest the true agenda of that particular party. It continues in a roundabout way to change the rules of the game and the process that all Canadian workers are familiar with. It creates uncertainty in the land between management and labour when it comes to the art of collective bargaining.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that time is short today and I do not want to tie this up. I want you to know that when all is said and done, this is not good legislation. I suppose it is the best we can put forward when you consider the ideology of the government. I hope that the arbitrator
chosen will have a tremendous sensitivity to the difficulties in Canada Post.
I want to make this very clear to all people who are listening out there today. The arbitration that was put in place in 1987 did not rectify the problems at Canada Post. The arbitration process that we are putting into effect here today through this back-to-work legislation will not rectify the problems at Canada Post. Only good faith bargaining can do that for Canada Post and its employees. I hope that people realize that the sooner we put that mechanism to work and allow them to improve their differences, the sooner we will get good postal service in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to say that this caucus is pleased that the minister took us seriously last night and understood the kind of concerns we were expressing. When the minister introduced his amendment today, he talked about good faith being shown by Canada Post. Based on what the letter that we tabled in a committee meeting last night said, there was a serious question about good faith. That letter really highlighted why we, the New Democratic Party caucus, were terribly concerned about what was in clause 7.
We appreciated the minister's arguments that what we were seeking in clause 7 was indeed already there. That was an assurance that clause 7, which talks about what would be taken into account by the arbitrator, would include the Gold mediation and the matters that were agreed to while the mediation took place. It would include the Lapointe conciliation report recommendations, at least in terms of looking at where they belong and not having them superimpose anything that was subsequently negotiated between the two parties with Mr. Gold, or subsequent to Mr. Gold reporting out, and any other discussions or substantive agreements that were made between the time Mr. Gold reported out and the time that this legislation becomes law. As you know the two parties continued to negotiate over the weekend. There were matters on which there was substantive agreement throughout the whole process and although they had been agreed to in principle, they had been sent away for drafting. In collective bargaining when there is an agreement in principle, material is sent away for drafting. When it comes back to the parties they review it
October 29, 1991

and at that point if they agree that the wording is appropriate, they sign it off.
In this instance because things moved rather quickly, there were a number of items that had been agreed to in principle and had been sent for drafting or were awaiting signing off. Matters overtook those items on the agenda and bargaining broke off.
We were concerned about those items that had not been signed off-although we were absolutely sure that the minister was correct when he said Canada Post was bargaining in good faith-because of the letter Mr. Parrot received at one o'clock yesterday afternoon, after the Postal Services Continuation Act was tabled in the House. The letter said, and I would like to read it:
During the course of these negotiations, in an effort to reach a negotiated collective agreement, and later in an effort to avoid a strike, with its costs and hardships caused by continued work disruptions, the corporation made several proposals and offers and agreed to various texts and positions. It now seems apparent at this late hour that this effort, including all the most recent concessions the corporation has made, has not helped us to attain our goal of a negotiated collective agreement.
This is to advise you that any and all of the corporation's positions, offers and proposals made through the mediator or otherwise, after midnight of August 23, 1991, are withdrawn. This includes any language, propositions, offers and proposals that were accepted by the union with the exception of clauses signed by the parties during the mediation process.
The corporation's position now reverts to the recommendations of the conciliation board, chaired by Mr. Lapointe.
Mr. Courville, Chief Negotiator, Canada Post.
We were somewhat alarmed when we saw a letter from Canada Post saying "everything that has been agreed to after the date of August 23 is now no longer in agreement", unless it has been signed off. Many, many items were substantially agreed to, both with the mediator, Mr. Gold, and in bargaining that took place with the two parties after Mr. Gold signed off.
So we are very, very pleased that the minister has taken account of our concerns and introduced this amendment to clause 7.
One of the important factors is that often those who have not participated in the collective bargaining process lose sight of the fluidity of bargaining. We understand
Government Orders
and surely the minister and both parties understand that when you are bargaining, things change. Something is offered in return for something being taken off the table, or something is agreed to in return for something else being put on the table.
In a definitive way to say that unless it is signed off it is not going to be covered by this bill would have been a disaster in terms of hours and hours and days and days and weeks and weeks of very tough bargaining on everyone's part. It is very important that the minister has introduced this amendment and is in fact allowing all of that hard and good work that was done to be taken into account by the arbitrator.
I think it is also very important at this report stage to know that there was another substantive clause that we expressed considerable concern about. That clause was clause 5, paragraphs (3)(a) and (3)(b). This clause in essence covers the time period that began August 24, 1991 and ended at 3 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time on September 5, 1991. At that period of time there was no collective agreement in effect. Rather than extending the collective agreement, the New Democratic members on the committee requested that the provisions in the collective agreement be used to deal with people who had been disciplined or discharged in that time period. The government has set those dates aside and provided a clause that does in fact provide for arbitration. However, it also provides that those people will not be returning to work or will not be at work while they are waiting for an arbitrated settlement.
We in Canada have always prided ourselves in an attitude of innocent until proven guilty. We have, the minister tells us, 71 people who will not be working at Canada Post until the arbitrated period is finalized for those people who were fired during that winter. What we have therefore is a situation whereby a number of workers who in some instances have been disciplined or discharged for very minor things will in fact be away from work for a long period of time. It has already been two months that those workers have been unable to attend work, have not received pay, are not eligible for unemployment insurance because they have been discharged or are not eligible for welfare in many provinces because they have been discharged. In fact they must now wait for an arbitrated process.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
The minister tells us he will facilitate a fairly quick review of those arbitrations. He will ask the arbitrator to facilitate a quick review and try to deal with those whose transgressions are of a more minor nature.
The fact remains that by leaving this clause as it is in section 5, we are taking the position that all those people who have been discharged had been discharged for good cause, are guilty of whatever they have been accused of and should therefore pay a further penalty.
We had asked that this section be amended by adding at clause (c) that the employee should be reinstated during implementation of the process under sections 3(a) and (b). We felt that it was a fairly simple but humane way to go. Last night the committee chose not to agree with us. I think it is very important that we remember the basic principle of innocent until proven guilty.
In conclusion, I would like to say that we would very much like to see this matter settled. We feel very strongly. We are opposed to this legislation. We are opposed to legislating people back to work before they have even gone on strike. In essence this legislation almost says: "We are taking away your right to strike".
It is very important once this legislation is completed and the arbitration process begins that the House of Commons and the committees that are responsible take a very serious look at collective bargaining in the federal sector. Under this government we have had back-to-work legislation nine times. Every time we get back-to-work legislation it is a further indictment of the failure of the collective bargaining process under the federal laws and under the federal government.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to engage in a few minutes of debate on this matter.
As I see it this has been a very interesting process, one in which I have maintained a considerable amount of interest. For the first couple of years of this Parliament I served as the New Democrats post office critic and have been very pleased with the results of the work of my colleagues the member for Churchill, our new post office critic, and the member for Mission-Coquitlam, our party's labour spokesperson. I believe that a lot of the work they have been doing in the last few weeks has
helped to build an understanding by members in this House and people across Canada of the collective bargaining process and its value in our society.
What we were seeing on our television news screens and in the pages of Canadian newspapers over the last little while has been the process of collective bargaining.
The Canada Post Corporation and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers have been sitting down daily for six weeks and going through word by word, clause by clause, and paragraph by paragraph parts of a very difficult matter, trying to negotiate a collective agreement, something that had failed on numerous occasions.
That collective bargaining process ended just a very few short days ago with all parties acknowledging that in fact they were very close to a settlement. The collective bargaining process had almost achieved a success in what has been a very difficult and long discussed process.
I felt very confident that in fact this matter would be settled through the collective bargaining process. Despite the fact that I have a great deal of concern about the direction that Canada Post has been taking in recent years, the move toward privatizing postal outlets and the privatizing of the whole retail network has been of great concern to me.
The use of contract and part-time employees was of great concern to me, as was the whole sense that management was expressing that in fact the workers were to blame for much of the problems at Canada Post and management direction was not the cause of any of the problem. Despite the fact that I have great concern in those areas, I was relieved to hear that among the many clauses in a potential collective agreement there was considerable agreement between parties.
I was most disturbed to see the letter-and my hon. colleague from Mission-Coquitlam raised it just a few moments ago-from Canada Post indicating that as far as it was concerned because of this legislation all agreements it had reached with members of the union after August 23 would be withdrawn. In fact, those hours of dedicated collective bargaining were virtually thrown out the window.

I cannot express strongly enough how disappointed I was that Canada Post, the management, the corporation, would say that in fact those negotiations were for nothing.
Therefore I thought the reasonableness of the process, the potential success of the process, just lost all credibility because the corporation was going to step backward and give up these matters which had been agreed to through the collective bargaining process and, had a final agreement been reached, would have been accepted happily by signing the collective agreement. With the bringing in of the stay-at-work legislation, this government has essentially allowed the corporation to maintain its position. I am quite happy to know that amendments are before us that will in fact clarify this matter further and perhaps will settle it.
I very much appreciate the work of all parties in this regard because there is nothing more difficult than reaching agreements in difficult situations, situations where emotions run high. There is no question that there are philosophical differences relating to this collective agreement as well as simply practical administrative matters. I have been listening carefully to the remarks that have been made in the House. I just want to put one thing on record that I think is most important before we go on in this process relating to this legislation. When the minister introduced this legislation he used in his justification words to the effect that seniors needed to get their cheques. I could not agree more.
The phone calls to my office indicated that a disruption in service at Canada Post would be most detrimental to the quality of life and the ability of those people on fixed incomes who rely on Canada Post to deliver that income to them to maintain their lives.
It was not necessary, I thought, to justify the stay-at-work legislation, given that Canada Post Corporation was presented with a suggestion by the Canadian Union of Postal Workers to ensure that the delivery of these cheques would be carried out. In fact my colleague, the member for Churchill and now the NDP's postal critic, was quite angered by Canada Post's refusal to ensure the cheques for senior citizens would be delivered by postal workers on their own time in the event of a disruption. Since September 19 my colleague from Churchill has been seeking Canada Post's participation in a protocol that CUPW had already agreed to. Such an agreement
Government Orders
would permit the delivery of cheques to those who rely on mail delivery for those cheques.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, because you have signalled me that my time is about to expire, I want to commend the process that has taken us to this point already, a process that seemed to indicate the successfulness of the collective bargaining process in this country and assure the seniors and others in my constituency that it is not the members of the union who are trying to prevent the delivery of their income to their doors. It is in fact a deliberate attempt by Canada Post to ensure that the blame again falls on the workers when perhaps the opposite is the case.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to say a few words here today. I am looking forward to seeing this matter settled in the interest of all Canadians and of ensuring that Canada Post Corporation and this government understand that indeed service to Canadians is the mandate of Canada Post and that Canadians deserve a strong service oriented post office to serve them.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having the opportunity to make a few short remarks on this very important piece of legislation.
I just want to say that when a corporation basically goes from losing almost $1 billion a year, as this corporation was prone to do in the early eighties, to generating I understand this year close to $300 million to $400 million there is a lot of excellent work obviously being done by both parties.
Management obviously is using its ingenuity in terms of technological change and making sure that there are efficiencies and productivity systems being put in place. At the same time we should not forget what productivity is. The capacity of machines is ultimately the exercise of the will, the co-operation and the support of the work force. We cannot forget that the work force within the postal system of Canada obviously has also done a fabulous job.
I speak as a small businessman who on more than one occasion has borne the brunt of having a negative experience as a result of not getting the mail delivered. I understand the frustration of small businesses in this country when postal service is disrupted. The problems that you have when you are trying to meet your payroll

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
and your payables and your mail does not come in are tough.
Often the letter carriers bear the brunt of abuse when we have a strike with the post office. I experienced a situation last summer in my riding of Broadview- Greenwood where the letter carriers were being publicly maligned because the pension cheques, welfare cheques and disability pension cheques were not being delivered. In our particular area, the stewards of postal stations J and G expressed in writing a willingness to say: "Listen, we do not want to see seniors standing out here in 110 degree heat. We want to deliver those cheques and we are willing to deliver them to those people who are in need, seniors who are having difficult times finding money to buy their groceries". It was a horrific scene on Danforth and on Carlisle last summer. There were single moms waiting for unemployment cheques.
There was a misunderstanding that crept into the community. Those people that were out there suffering tended to blame the letter carriers when in fact they were willing to try and ameliorate the situation.
I can remember communicating with the executives of the post office who said: "Well, no, we are not going to co-operate on this unless all cheques or all mail right across the country is delivered". In other words, it was an almost all or nothing approach. I remember a specific situation where I was out there chatting with some of my seniors. On one particular day a senior citizen nearly passed out almost right in front of me. I called Mr. Lander and tried to express my concern to him: "Listen, I am absolutely convinced that you and your management team are not supporting this kind of action". This is what happens. Sometimes we become remote from the real suffering that is out there. Sometimes we are too quick to blame those who seemingly are on the front lines. In this particular case, I felt that there was a lot of unnecessary abuse being handed out toward our letter carriers.
It seems that there has been a good spirit developed here in this process of negotiation, but I hope that both sides will park their tactical resources and their little jousting resources that they have and get into the spirit that seems to exist in this House today. The minister has expressed so clearly today that both sides seem to be
sincere in solving this issue. I think if we can continue that spirit then the people of Canada will ultimately be the beneficiaries.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say on Bill C-40.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the legislative committee met last night, late into the night, to work through this bill and to seek the consensus that we felt was necessary to produce passage of this bill today in the House.
We did have some disagreement last night, but at the end of the evening I think we were close to unanimous. We agreed that we had a willing minister who was willing to listen to both sides of the argument and who was willing to take some of our considerations to his people very early this morning in an attempt to come up with a bill that we could all support in this House today. He did that. One of the concerns expressed last night, and articulated this morning by the member for Mission- Coquitlam, was simply that we did not want to lose much of what has been accomplished up to this point through the conciliation process.
Although the members of the committee from the government side, including the minister, felt that the bill as presented yesterday would do the job, there was concern by the NDP and the Liberal committee members that Bill C-40 would not accomplish that.
In the best sense of compromise, the minister did go back to his people and his legal counsel. He told us last evening that he would attempt to bring in an amendment to Bill C-40, particularly clause 7, in the hopes of relieving some of the anxiety postal workers experienced, and felt they would experience, if we did not change that part of the legislation.
The minister did that. From the expressions from the various sides of the House this morning, we would have to agree that he kept his word and did a good job in coming up with a bill that we on both sides of this House should be able to support.
We do not want to lose sight of what Bill C-40 does. It is the legislation that will put the postal workers back to work in the event of a strike. It appears that strike is coming very, very soon. The point of the legislation is to put the postal workers back to work, to do what all Canadians want them to do, deliver the mail.
October 29, 1991

As I mentioned yesterday in the House, 80 per cent of the mail in this country is business mail. We can think of all kinds of things that can destroy a business. We can talk about inflation, high interest rates and a high Canadian dollar. But the fact is, if we do not have mail delivery, that in itself can destroy a Canadian business. It has done so in many cases.
I have had some dialogue with some business people in my constituency. They are, of course, of the same opinion that mail delivery to their business is very, very critical. We cannot afford another strike, short or lengthy.
I want to congratulate the minister. I think he has conducted himself on a very, very high level in a very, very difficult situation to ensure that the passage of this bill does take place. Again, the objective is to make sure that Canadians have good, continuous postal service. The country at this particular time, coming through a recession, cannot afford a postal strike, whether it is short term or long term.
I believe we have accomplished that in the legislation and in the amendment the minister brought before this House this morning. I am sure that the majority of members in this House can support the back-to-work legislation.

Mr. Speaker, looking at this legislation and considering the ramifications it will have for the Canadian public, we can accept the fact that service to Canadians is the paramount issue with regard to Canada Post.
Last evening all three parties had an opportunity to sit and listen to the presentations from Canada Post, CUPW and the minister, and to discuss the issues that are forthcoming today.
We also felt very concerned about some of the issues that came up yesterday afternoon.
I refer in particular to the letter from Canada Post which basically withdrew its total position through the mediation process and its position ever since August 16, where the conciliation had occurred.
I have to commend very much the minister for the position that he took in making certain that we are not going to overlook Mr. Gold's work. He did a tremendous amount of work in bringing together many of the unresolved issues. The mediation process, as the minis-
Govemment Orders
ter pointed out, was very successful. We are very pleased that that did occur.
I guess today we look at the amendment that the minister brought in to make certain that that mediation process is at least taken into account by the arbitrator. The arbitrator will not be going back to square one as CUPW was very concerned about, with very good reason I might point out.
We are very happy that when we spoke with Mr. Parrot he told us that if we could make certain that the conciliation process and the mediation process were guaranteed to come in line, and those areas that had been agreed to by both parties were in place, then arbitration could settle the few outstanding issues that remain.
I really see no other way to settle them at this point. I would support what the minister has said. We had come to a point in the mediation where maybe each party was at the very bottom line whereby no further movement, or not much further movement, would occur. As a result, in his wisdom he left the process to move to a further finalization through an arbitrator.
The minister in following that up did that quite appropriately for avoiding a strike and making sure that proper protection for each party was paramount.
At the same time, I have to congratulate the member for Kenora-Rainy River who worked so diligently at bringing forth an amendment to meet that need. It made certain we did not go back to the beginning of mediation, go back to the point they were at in the middle of the summer. He worked very diligently at drafting an amendment to make certain that the minister and everyone understood that we should be using all of the work of mediation and bringing it through. I think it was through the diligent work of my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River that that came about. So I would commend him very much.
I commend the minister for taking several hours to sit down last night and go through the bill clause by clause, explain the implications of the bill, try to listen very carefully to the arguments and come up with a resolution that all parties could accept.
I did, and I still do, have a couple of concerns with the bill. The first concern that I would voice is the fact that we have some 70 workers who basically over the strike period of time, the 10 days, have been suspended or put

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
out of work. They are not being given an opportunity to be reinstated immediately. I think there are some of these individuals who, through one means or another, were dismissed improperly. They should not be found guilty before the hearing is actually held in their favour. However, the bill does address some of that and possibly will not lead them to the point of coming to the end of all the arbitration. There are 130,000 arbitration cases or grievances that have to come forward, so that process will be speeded up somewhat.
The other area I did have some concern about, and I voice this directly to the minister as well, is the fact that you are referring the arbitrator to Canada Post's corporate plan. I personally do not see any reason to prejudice the arbitrator by suggesting the corporate plan should be part of the arbitration process. I certainly believe that in putting parties up equally, the CUPW group and Canada Post should be able to present their concerns and their arguments on an equal footing. To make it a direction of this bill that the arbitrator consider the Canada Post corporate plan seems to me to bias a neutral position this bill should take in the resolution of this problem that is there.
I do think that we have stilted the arbitrator's opinions somewhat by mentioning the Canada Post corporate plan. However, again I would suggest very strongly that all parties, all individuals, worked together very well last evening and I would give congratulations to everyone involved, particularly my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River and the minister and I would say the NDP for its efforts with that as well.

Mr. Speaker, I probably will be congratulating the minister at the end of my speech as well, but I would like to congratulate him at the beginning along with my colleagues, the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Churchill, and yes indeed the Liberals too for the work which they did, particularly last night in getting some changes to the bill which certainly are going to go a long way toward ameliorating the problem which we find ourselves in today as far as the labour dispute and the contractual problems with Canada Post and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers are concerned.
Nonetheless, Mr. Speaker, I sat in on the committee last night. It is the first time I had been in one of those
committees since the back-to-work legislation for the ships' crews and the hospital workers and the Public Service Alliance strike of a while ago. It is amazing how little things change with time.
What we see in the whole labour relations with adjuncts of the government such as the post office is a willingness on behalf of these branches of the government to try to be absolved of the major responsibility for really good faith bargaining when they come to negotiating with their employees.
I think the best way to sum that up is that they depend in all instances, it seems to me, during negotiations for the government to get them off the hook if something fails and they really do not care whether they fail or not. I think the situation we find ourselves in now is ample evidence of that.
I would suggest however that with the bill before us, particularly the amendment which we are discussing right now, in actual fact the government has put the responsibility particularly back on Canada Post. I would only have wished that this kind of philosophy, this kind of attitude, this kind of mind-set, had been part of the negotiations which started at the beginning. I do not think that what is happening here is that the government has for the most part got Canada Post off the hook on this issue.
There certainly was an indication that that might be what was happening in the original legislation. It is to the credit of the minister and his sensitivity for particularly the people involved as workers at Canada Post that we have this amendment.
Clause 7 would have for all intents and purposes negated everything which had occurred up until the implementation of this legislation. It gave a whole new meaning and a whole new weight to that expression where it says we have to go back to square one, although it would not have been quite square one because we did have the conciliator's report in between which did make a few recommendations but in no way was definitive or addressed the major problems of the postal workers. Hence, we of course had the strike. Clause 7 was the reference to where if the parties were not able to agree they would go back to the conciliator's report, ignoring the excellent amount of work which was accomplished under the leadership of Judge Gold. Those of us who watch our news reports almost on a daily basis were able
October 29, 1991

to sense that after Judge Gold became involved in the negotiations, a tremendous amount of progress was made. It certainly is to his credit as well that that occurred. I suspect also, with the respect in which he is held by both parties, he is to be tremendously credited for having accomplished that much.
The fact of the matter is that without the intervention of the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Churchill and, yes, to some extent as well the member for Kenora-Rainy River, progress was made last night. The minister was able to be apprised of some of the sensitivities which were involved and I think for the most part the absolute stupidity of ignoring everything which had been accomplished up to that point, including what had occurred between Canada Post and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers subsequent to Judge Gold's leaving the scene in what I suspect was a certain degree of frustration. Nonetheless, as has been indicated in more than one instance, they were very close to coming to a settlement. There were not all that many outstanding issues.
I am not privy necessarily to what those instances were, but I suspect that the legislation which we have before us this morning will go a long way toward solving those issues as well.
There is at least one other part of the legislation to which I would like to refer. It is unfortunate that were was not more progress made in so far as clause 5 was concerned. Clause 5 refers to the action which will be taken regarding those who in the opinion of Canada Post have violated Canada Post's sensitivities in so far as people should conduct themselves on the picket line.
I would suggest that it is tremendously unfortunate that some other form of amelioration of that problem was not brought forward, other than just simply the assurance of the minister, which I do not doubt, where he says those cases will be followed expeditiously. Even so, these people have been without any sort of income for two months. It is difficult to say how long the process will take for the arbitrator to arrive at a decision in their instance. I would suspect that some of them are suffering tremendously and their families are suffering tremendous hardships as result of Canada Post acting as judge and jury and for all intents and purposes sentencing these people to what may very well be a very heavy fine,
Government Orders
albeit imposed by it through the withdrawal of their wages.
I would like to emphasize in relation to this whole matter of those who have been disciplined by any company in a situation such as this, for the most part when the dust settles, however far it is into the future after a settlement, often when a settlement is arrived at the union says: "All these people come back or none of us come back", and of course that is a stance which very quickly solves the matter. I think it is to Canada Post's everlasting shame that they did not agree to that.
In 1987 in a similar situation, 42 people had been similarly disciplined, summarily discharged by Canada Post, only to have 38 of those 42 people-or close to those numbers-reinstated which means for all intents and purposes the charges against them were withdrawn. That is tremendously common.
In this 1991 instance, we have 71 people. I can predict right now that probably at least 65 of those will be found to be completely innocent of the charges which Canada Post has brought against them and for which it has acted as judge, jury and hangman.
I really hope that in the case of these people the minister uses his influence to expedite these tremendously sensitive problems these people have as quickly as possible. I even hope that without his interference, Canada Post will take a second look and read the report of last night's committee, read what was said, what was pleaded in relation to those people and reinstate them.
As a matter of fact, there was the case of a part-time worker employed during the strike-we could use more impolite terms-who was charged by Canada Post but continued to work. If substitute employees can continue to work, I would suggest that full-time employees can too.

Mr. Speaker, we are in the House today to discuss the Postal Services Continuation Act. This morning, I had a chance to talk to several constituents from my riding of Saint-Maurice, who were under the impression that the government not only wanted to maintain postal services and avoid a strike at all costs, but also wanted to impose all the working conditions for Canada Post employees. That is what people are saying, and it seems this rumour is widespread. However, if we take a closer look at the legislation proposed by the Minister of Labour, it is in fact

Government Orders
quite moderate. It is a very acceptable piece of legislation that, of course, is intended to maintain postal services-I don't think there is any doubt about that among most Canadians-but this legislation will also enable the parties to agree on a certain number of items that are still in dispute and could not be dealt with in the past. So first of all, I think we should make it clear to Canadians that the government has no intention of forcing measures down anyone's throat. It just wants our Canadian postal system to function properly.
Listeners may wonder why we are again stuck in this country with a deadlock in negotiations between the Canada Post Corporation and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. It is a serious problem, and unfortunately, no one in this House has a solution. We could consider the history of the founding of the Canada Post Corporation and also relations prior to that event, to try and understand. However, this is probably one of society's greatest mysteries, and I certainly do not have the answer.
There were people, especially among the opposition, who tried to argue that it was not appropriate to pass legislation at this time, and that perhaps we should wait a little longer. I beg to differ. I think that Canadians, the people we are supposed to represent, have been extremely patient. Mr. Speaker, these negotiations have been going on for nearly two years. They have been talking for 23 months. The process included 78 conciliation meetings, 60 meetings arranged by the Conciliation Board, and 40 mediation meetings with Judge Alan B. Gold. Mr. Speaker, that is a lot of talking. Furthermore, all these discussions cost Canadian taxpayers a lot of money, since they have to pay the bills for negotiations which have been going on for two years.
I find it very difficult to understand why some opposition members say the government should wait a little longer. They say the government should allow another strike and let the Canadian postal system be disrupted again. I do not agree, Mr. Speaker. There are many people in my riding who think this legislation may not be drastic enough and may not be the kind of legislation we need in the circumstances. I am not saying I share this position, but Canadians are becoming exasperated. Many people would appreciate a firmer approach.
However, it is a nice surprise, I must say, to see the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party both commend the Minister of Labour for the way he acted in introducing this special legislation, and especially for his efforts since last August to reason with both parties and facilitate a settlement. This is quite a positive attitude on their part.
It must be made clear that the personal involvement of the Minister of Labour was most helpful. He managed to convince the parties to bargain on good faith a whole slew of items regarding this collective agreement. Unfortunately, we find ourselves today, Mr. Speaker, in a situation where the negotiations between the Canadian Postal Workers Union and Canada Post have stalled again.
Parliament could pass back-to-work legislation to at least maintain postal services, since, technically, there is no strike. We could even impose new work agreements for the next few years on the workers, without consulting them, as the Quebec government did a while back.
I think that this would not be a good idea, however favourably some view this solution. We are giving the CUPW and Canada Post enough leeway, Mr. Speaker, to pass special legislation quickly with the unanimous consent of this House while allowing Canada Post employees to get relatively interesting working conditions.
It is not to ridicule the postal workers or to be envious of them than to say that their working conditions are very good, with a great pension plan and fringe benefits like few Canadians get in their collective agreements.
Mentioning this is arrogant and saying that postal workers have always been well treated is the truth, Mr. Speaker, and I think that we should repeat it to Canadians today.
The other point on which I would like to speak briefly is that a few weeks ago, we had a postal strike that disrupted services nationwide, in spite of the efforts made by management to maintain those services. But there is a more fundamental problem, namely the increasing competition faced by Canada Post. Courier companies, electronic mail systems, telephone companies in general as well as oral communications have been expanding in Canada and throughout the world in the
October 29, 1991

last ten years. This makes it much more difficult for Canada Post. The Corporation must face the competition.
Mr. Speaker, every time there is a strike at Canada Post, contracts which were obtained with difficulty by the officials of the Corporation are in jeopardy. Indeed, these contracts could be lost by Canada Post which would have the effect of jeopardizing the employees part-time or full-time jobs.
Since we live in an increasingly competitive and interdependent world, the Canada Post Corporation and its employees can no longer behave, Mr. Speaker, as though they had a total monopoly and control over the handling of postal services across the country. This is an aspect to which the Government of Canada must pay the greatest attention, since the two parties were unable to reach an agreement.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I must tell the union members in my riding that I believe very firmly and clearly in the collective bargaining process and the right to strike. In my opinion, those are two essential rights in our society. However, when exercising those rights threatens the very future of Canada Post and of a number of jobs in that corporation and affects our companies' competitiveness, the government must intervene.
Small businesses in Canada account for 80 per cent of the new jobs created in 1991. Everything points to this trend continuing in years to come, Mr. Speaker. Considering the problems caused by the recession, as well as the economic problems in Canada, in the United States and all over the world, adding a new problem for small businesses, a strike by the postal workers, would make it much harder for them to compete. These difficulties must be overcome and that is why the government has brought in this Act to provide for the continuation of postal services, with all that entails, but also with advantages for postal workers who should seriously consider the open-mindedness of the Minister of Labour. The minister should be congratulated for his efforts in recent weeks. Since my time is nearly up, Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by wishing very sincerely that the Parliament of Canada, the House of Commons and the Senate, unanimously and very quickly pass the 1991 Act to provide for the continuation of postal services,
Government Orders
and that we can again receive normal postal services for a very long time.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to stand today and speak on this bill before the House.
It appears that this is a situation where we have to review exactly where we are going in the Public Service sector. We have to review where we are going in the area of labour relations. It seems to me that what we have seen lately in legislating people back to work, I believe it is four times since the last throne speech, is a labour relations situation from the dark ages.
We have to face up to the fact that we are going into the 21st century. We as legislators and particularly the government must realize and recognize that there are other ways of doing things than the old confrontational methods that we have seen used by Mr. Lander of Canada Post and by the Minister of Finance with his zero rate increase in the Public Service sector. There is a way of approaching a collective agreement and collective bargaining in good faith and looking at all aspects of the people, the job and the industry in which they are in, in the service sector, the Public Service sector and again in the postal service.
We have a situation where the postal union has been without a contract for some period of time. It has been looking and trying to bargain in good faith on the part of the employees, but there is that frustration factor present.
If we look at what has happened over the last few years, the so-called privatization of Canada Post, the closing of rural post offices, the gutting of the rural system of postal delivery, this was done without asking for any input from the members of the postal union or the employees of that union or of the corporation.
It seems to me that if we are going to go into the future in a way that does away with strikes, as so many people in this country wish for, we have to look at the situation and take input from all sectors. We must not only listen to management, or the union and employees or the government. We must look at the situation from all sides and take input from all sides to come to a conclusion.

Government Orders
It is not good enough any more, as we have done in Canada Post, to ignore the employees' side and take the management side and say: "We are going to streamline the system."
I have spoken to letter carriers, postal workers and managers of small post offices within my riding and other ridings. It is clear that these people who work every day delivering, sorting our mail and getting it to us in a timely manner, know how the system works and know how it can be improved, but are they asked for their input? Are they asked how the system can be made better so that service can improve, so that we as taxpayers can save some of the tax dollars with the improvements? No, they are not asked.
The input they could give is ignored. In today's climate, that is simply not good enough. We have to start asking those workers for their input. We have to start taking into consideration all aspects of what management, employees and those who are being served want and need. This is the way of the future. This is what we have to start looking at.
In the minister's comments yesterday he spoke, and probably rightfully so, about some of the difficulties the citizens of Canada and certainly the people in my area are concerned about. I have a very high percentage of seniors in the Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt and the boundary country of my riding of well over 30 per cent. They depend on regular delivery of mail to keep in touch with their neighbours, their friends and relatives and to get their old age security, Canada Pension and various other pension cheques.
The solution has been put forward more than once by the member for Churchill. The members of the postal union offered to make an agreement between the union and management to ensure that the uncertainty of the delivery of these cheques be taken into consideration ahead of time. Then everyone would know what was going to happen and that these cheques would be delivered to the people who so badly need them.
What did management do? They turned their back on it. They turned their back on the senior citizens and said:
"We will wait until we see what happens". Well, the precedent was set in the past. Management agreed in the past to a regular transitional period where service would be continued. Why will Canada Post not agree to it this time around? Why have we got this confrontational edge once again?
If we think back on confrontation we can look at the last postal strike where the postal service trained people as scabs to take over jobs of legitimate employees and union members ahead of any strike notification. It seems that the 19th century method of dealing with employees was once again at the forefront: negotiation by confrontation. For those people in my constituency, that is not satisfactory. I am sure that for most people sitting in the House of Commons that is not satisfactory. For senior citizens, the small business person and those in large industries, that is no longer satisfactory.
We have to look at what must be done. We must get away from confrontation within the labour relations area. We must negotiate in good faith from the beginning and before the collective agreement expires. It is not good enough to wait until two weeks, two months or two years after the fact to begin negotiating seriously. We must look at negotiating from the beginning and go through it.
I do wish to look briefly at some of the legislation to make it known exactly what has happened here. As I understand it, the minister is to appoint an arbitrator through interventions by the member for Churchill and the member for Mission-Coquitlam. The minister has brought in a recent amendment to clause 7(2)(b) of the bill wherein he allows any substantial agreement that has already been reached on other matters, including salaries, to be incorporated in the collective agreement under the arbitration. Then we do not have to go back to square one as it were in trying to reach an agreement under arbitration. That is a major step.
It seems to me that much has been gained over the last six weeks through Mr. Justice Gold as mediator and the union and management. It would be a pity to lose that under the present legislation. I am very pleased that the minister has recognized that and has brought in this reasoned amendment.

I hope for the sake of all Canadians that reason will prevail, that Canada Post and the union will get down to negotiating in good faith, that the employer, Canada Post, will not continue its confrontational methods and will make every attempt to reach a satisfactory agreement. Seniors and small business people across the country will then be served in the manner that they are deserving of.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking on third reading of this particular legislation, Bill C-40, there has been a great deal of co-operation since this bill was first talked about by the various political parties in terms of this particular piece of legislation, particularly when it went on notice as of last week.
We had suggested all through this particular dispute that it could be resolved by having a third independent party come in to assess the various concerns with regard to postal services as well as monetary issues between the employees and management.
Government Orders
It was not until the eleventh hour that the Government of Canada came to its senses and appointed a mediator who worked very hard. I understand from the information that has come to my attention that representatives of the Canadian Union of Postal Employees as well as representatives of management attempted in a very sincere way to resolve many of their outstanding differences.
I think it should be clearly understood that labour and to a similar extent management attempted in good faith to resolve their outstanding differences.
I want to say on the record on behalf of my party that we believe wholeheartedly in the collective bargaining process. We want to compliment the participants in the process for coming together with Justice Gold and agreeing on many-I want to underline-many of the outstanding matters that were previously between the two parties.
I think it is important that we recognize that, and applaud the parties and also Justice Gold who tried to consummate an agreement.
Events prior to the appointment of Justice Gold made it in our view very difficult for the parties to consummate a collective agreement. There are many reasons why.
We have the example of management saying to workers with regard to monetary issues and job security that certain things could not go their way. On the other hand, we find that the monetary increases for the president of Canada Post, for the job security of the president of Canada Post were very rich and very rich indeed.
I do not know the exact amounts. I do not have the Order in Council before me, but I am led to believe that it is in the magnitude of $100,000 in terms of salary increase.
Mr Speaker, I want to say to you as the arbitrator, as the individual who is impartial in this Chamber and has the respect of all members, that as much as I respect and admire the Chair, I could not understand or see myself voting in favour of a $100,000 raise for the Chair.
Now, we have the president of Canada Post who is going to get a sizeable increase. There is a colleague in my caucus who phrased it quite well. It is pay-off for

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
lay-off. We also have the situation with regard to the proliferation of closures of rural post offices across this country.
I know members opposite do not really care about rural Canada. They do not really care about those communities, whether they be in Ontario, Quebec or western Canada or in Atlantic Canada. This was another example of the government's economic agenda through the agency of Canada Post which made it very difficult for the parties to consummate an agreement.
The government has had direct involvement in this process because it has been pulling the strings. It has been pulling the strings all along. It was not the Canadian Union of Public Employees which moved an Order in Council to increase the salary of the president of Canada Post.
It was not the union nor its representatives who moved a motion or an Order in Council to give a substantial bonus to the president of Canada Post, was it? It was the members opposite.
The government House leader is the minister responsible. The Minister of Labour must bear part of the responsibility, and of course other things have come into play. They are indirect but in another way it could be argued they affect directly the negotiation in terms of the proliferation of taxes and inflation in the high dollar. What do working men and women do in those kinds of situations?
They have to seek monetary increases. They have to seek some degree of job security for their memberships and the families of those memberships. I know all members, notwithstanding their political partisan stripe, would have to concur that that is a very, very important aspect of the collective bargaining process. It became very difficult, if not impossible. We realized shortly thereafter that it would eventually break down.
There are serious discussions of individuals who have brought to my attention that perhaps the government while negotiations were proceeding wanted to have this particular strike. I do not know how authentic that is, but it is certainly an aspect that we must give serious consideration to.
My colleagues in debate, both in this particular debate as well as in previous debates, have mentioned on the floor of this House that perhaps a commission of inquiry ought to take place with regard to the outstanding
grievances at Canada Post that go back for some time and that are disturbing, not only to union representatives and their employees, but I would suspect to middle management of Canada Post, and certainly to the Canadian public.
We need to have an airing of those concerns. We have to breathe fresh air into a process which seems to have broken down. If that is not followed through with, I suggest that we are going to have continual difficulties with that Crown corporation. We are going to have individuals feeling unfairly aggrieved in the process.
I would hope that the minister would give due consideration to the recommendation and the plea that we have made repeatedly on the floor of the House of Commons in terms of a commission of inquiry in order to resolve, once and for all, the problems at that particular corporation.
I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without making reference to some.of the words which were echoed in this Chamber by the minister responsible for Canada Post. He said earlier this week, and I believe late last week, that Canada Post was the most efficient postal facility in the world.
What he has failed to tell the Canadian people is of the large number of Canadian businesses which have opted out of Canada Post and which are using private couriers in this country. He has failed to say on the floor of this House of Commons how certain institutions are being affected. I am going to give one example which has come to my attention within the last 24 hours. Medical schools in the province of Ontario have had to place the following words in their application form for the purposes of applicants: "Due to the slow delivery of mail, candidates are advised to submit their application several weeks in advance of this date. Registered mail or courier service is advised if a receipt is required. Collect courier deliveries will not be accepted."
So much for the minister's puffery about efficiency. We have an example here in Canada of medical schools in the province of Ontario saying to applicants: "If you are going to mail in your application, make sure you do it umpteen weeks in advance".
I find the comments of the minister opposite to be ludicrous. I also suggest a very impolite term, not one that I would subscribe to but it has been subscribed to me by others. This is very misleading for members of Parliament to be told this puffball story by the minister responsible.
October 29, 1991

My colleague, the critic, and his colleagues who have worked diligently with regard to this particular situation were co-operative throughout the piece. We made a recommendation last night in committee with regard to strengthening clause 7 to enable the arbitrator, whoever she or he may be, to enter the deliberations without having a hand tied behind their back. Unfortunately the minister did not see fit last night to accept clause by clause word by word our amendment. But I think he has gone a long way today to accept the intent, the pith and substance of our amendment last night. That is why we on this side have concurred whole-heartedly with the amendment and that it should be passed as it relates to clause 7.
There is no question about the difficulties between the two sides. That has been given in evidence by many speakers. We also have to talk about the public interest. Is the public being served? Will the public be served by a strike across this land? Will it facilitate business? I am not talking about the business cronies of the Minister of Labour who happen to live in the plush regions of the country. I am talking about the small business person who happens to be in northern Ontario. I am talking about the small business which happens to be in Regina, in Gander, Newfoundland, in Nova Scotia or Kenora- Rainy River. Will they be served if there is a strike? The answer is no. I do not think they will be served.
I would hope that this serves a lesson to the government and the political masters of Canada Post Corporation. This could all have been avoided if the government had seen the way it has provoked labour over the last number of years. It is not just through the collective bargaining process. You cannot look at that in isolation.
As I said earlier, there are a number of factors that compound the collective bargaining process whether it be the proliferation of taxes, the elimination of job security for employees which is involved in the collective bargaining process, the monetary elements or the nonmonetary elements. This government, in my view, has done a terrible job. I am sure the Minister of Labour in a quiet moment in his study would want to reflect on what
Government Orders
I am going to say and perhaps even agree that his government up to the present has been extremely incompetent in managing labour and management issues in Canada.
The Minister of Labour will stand in his place and say: "Oh, yes, but there have been in excess of 80 to 90 collective agreements signed in this country". That is true, but I make reference to the Public Service Alliance of Canada over which he has direct control. They have a great measure of control with regard to the Canada Post union employees. What has happened in those incidents is that we have seen time and time again that the collective bargaining process has broken down.
We believe that this could have been avoided. Notwithstanding that case, I have to say that we will be supporting this legislation on third reading because we believe it to be in the public interest. The minister should not think for one moment that we concur, we consent, we applaud in any way whatsoever the way in which this government has conducted the whole of labour-management relations in this country, and particularly as it relates to Canada Post. I want to make that perfectly clear.
There is clearly a public interest here, as I am sure the minister will want to attest to, and that must be met. We in this party will not be irresponsible. We believe that the parties must come together with the arbitrator and resolve these the outstanding matters expeditiously and fairly. We must keep in mind the undertakings that have been given by the Minister of Labour to the representatives of the Canadian Union of Public Employees as well as senior members of management to do that fairly.
I want to say in conclusion that we will be supporting this bill on third reading because of the public interest.
In no way do we accept, in no way do we acknowledge, in no way would we applaud the behaviour of the government in its efforts to bring labour and management to the table in an environment which is conducive to having collective bargaining in this country. It is very important across the land to bring them together in order that they may consummate their agreements without the involvement of the national government.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, on third reading of Bill C-40, I would like to start by thanking the Leader of the Official Opposition for his party's support for this legislation. Mr. Speaker, as you know it is never a pleasant task when a Minister of Labour has to table special legislation to end a labour dispute. However, I believe this is an exceptional case. As you know, the collective agreement expired on July 31, 1989. At the time, the Department of Labour appointed an experienced conciliator, Mr. Courchesne of Montreal, in an attempt to bring the parties closer together. Unfortunately, after more than 60 meetings involving Mr. Courchesne and the parties in question, no agreement was reached.
Subsequently, the Department of Labour appointed a conciliation board, with Mr. Desmarais as the Postal Union's representative and Mr. Arnold Masters for Canada Post, the employer. Both parties agreed to appoint Mr. Marc Lapointe, a distinguished Canadian and former president of the Canada Labour Relations Board, as chairman of the conciliation board. The board met and sat for nearly 23 months. It held over 70 meetings and made considerable progress, but was unable to persuade the parties to reach an agreement. At this point, the government could either introduce special legislation or make further efforts to try and get the parties together, and that is what we did. I got in touch with the person I consider to be the best mediator in the country, the Chief Justice of the Quebec Superior Court, Judge Alan B. Gold. Judge Gold's experience in a number of areas, including labour relations, is extraordinary, and he has settled a number of major labour disputes in Canada in the past. Judge Gold met the parties for nearly seven weeks. When the judge finally withdrew from the mediation process, he argued that even if he decided to stay on, he did not think the parties would be able to reach an agreement.

Therefore, the government has gone the extra mile in this dispute by first appointing the conciliation commissioner, the conciliation board and the best mediator in Canada, Judge Gold.
At the beginning of this dispute I understand that there were 310 issues that separated the parties; 260 of
them at the request of CUPW and Mr. Parrot, and 50 of them at the request of Canada Post.
I am told that in the three stages the conciliation commissioner, the conciliation board and the mediator settled and agreed upon over 90 per cent of the items in dispute. This bill covers the items on which they could not reach an agreement. I have been told by both sides which ones cannot be agreed upon.
In all fairness, I have heard both sides of the issue separately from the parties. I feel that maybe with a little more effort some of these issues could be settled. I also understand that on one issue they are far apart and it appears to be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to settle.
Having considered all that, I have come to the conclusion on behalf of the government that the way to settle the issue would be through Bill C-40 which would provide for the appointment of an arbitrator to impose the things they cannot agree on. They cannot agree on a number of issues, not because they do not negotiate in good faith, not because they are not sincere, I believe they are sincere. I do believe they negotiated in good faith and I was told by Judge Gold that they did negotiate in good faith.
If you consider that, I feel the bill that we have here, including the amendment that this House agreed to this morning, is a fair and reasonable bill and once it becomes law it will put an end to the dispute.
I do appeal at this time to Mr. Parrot, the president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, to have his people back at work. This has been going on for 23 months. I do understand and he kept his word. We did get the 24-hour notice for a strike. I understand now that some people are on strike across the country, but it is not the case in all places. With the co-operation of this House and with the co-operation of the other place, we will have this bill as law hopefully by the end of the day. I do appeal to him on behalf of the people of Canada to have his people back to work later tonight.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our caucus and especially our labour critic, the member for Mission-Coquitlam, I think it is very important to understand the process that has been going

on for the last couple of days outside of this House and inside of this House.
When the mediation broke down late last week, we recognized that there still was an opportunity for the parties to get together and try and resolve the dispute. Both parties to the collective agreement had press conferences indicating that they had come very close to an agreement. I, for one, think that the efforts undertaken by the minister and others to have the two sides get together on the weekend, even though they did not come to an agreement, were useful because it did give them a chance to air some of the issues that were still in dispute.
I think that process has helped with what happened yesterday and earlier today in this House. We have an indication, as a result of the amendment that the minister agreed to and introduced into this House earlier today, that there can be a quick settlement to this dispute. It is my understanding that even prior to the legislation passing the Senate that Jean-Claude Parrot is going to ask his members to return as soon as they can.
That does not mean that it will happen instantaneously. We have a number of different time zones and we have a number of different shifts for postal workers right across this country, but I think it is an indication of good faith that the union is not waiting for the legislation to pass the Senate but is taking all the possible steps to try and have its members go back to work. I applaud them for that move.
We will not support this legislation because we have some fundamental disagreements with items that are in the legislation. We also have a concern with the government's corporate agenda. Even though that is not in the legislation, that is cause for a lot of the disputes that have occurred in the Public Service this year. The agenda of privatization, the agenda of contracting out, the agenda of reducing the level of services to Canadians right across this land has meant that we have had more Public Service strikes in this last year than we have had in the last five years. It has meant that four of the last 40 pieces of legislation that have been introduced into this House of Commons have been back to work legislation, 10 per cent of the government's entire legislative package over the last few months. The two parties did come very close to an agreement. It was very important that in
Government Orders
the legislation that will pass this House in a few minutes that the amendment the minister brought forward was introduced.
There was a danger, and I do not think it was a danger purposely put there by the government, but there was a danger that we would have had a clause that would have really tied the hands of the arbitrator. We would have been in a situation under the previous wording where the arbitrator, if he could not find agreement on the items dealt with through mediation, would be forced to go to the conciliation board report and recommendation.
As proof of that, almost immediately Canada Post wrote a letter saying that it withdrew all the offers it had made since August 23, 1991. In other words, it was basically trying to force the arbitrator's hand to go back to the conciliation board report. That meant that we would have lost all the progress that had been made on major issues in the last two months; progress on child care, pensions for part-time employees, agreement on a wage package. In addition to those items, the two parties had worked and had come to an agreement in principle on a number of items dealing with issues and job security to the number of casual workers. Those were very important for the future peace in Canada Post.
It is important that that work not be lost. It was very important that in committee last night and in the House today the minister made it clear that whoever is chosen as an arbitrator must look at the work that was done in mediation and post mediation. That work is too important to be lost. It is very clear as a result of the amendment we have now and the speech by the minister that that is the primary goal of the arbitrator.
Yes, look at the conciliation board, but do not stop at the report of the conciliation board. Tike advantage of all the agreements that have occurred since the conciliation board made its report on August 16. It is not only good news in terms of the fact that we will have a very short strike, but it is good news in terms of the long term peace and security and service within Canada Post.
I applaud the minister for being flexible. I applaud both parties for the work they have done to make this possible. I regret that we did have to introduce back-to-work legislation, but that is a result as I said earlier of the government's political agenda.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
At the same time, what has happened in this House and what has happened over the last two days outside this House in committee meetings and meetings my colleague from Mission-Coquitlam had with the minister that we have achieved the best deal possible. I would hope the two parties can work to resolve the outstanding issues in very short order.
Also, it is important, as the minister indicated in his speech today, that Canada Post and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers meet early to make sure that the wage settlement that had been agreed to over the weekend be put into place quickly. These employees have already waited two years, since their collective agreement expired. We know that the arbitration process could take, three, four, five or six months. I do not think it would be fair to the employees to have to wait that long to get the pay increase that had been agreed to in committee.
We look forward to the end of this debate. [Translation]

The hon. member for Hull-Aylmer, on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put to the members of this House, I have a few comments. I agree that the government should act as quickly as possible to settle this dispute and allow the arbitration process to proceed. However, Mr. Speaker, there is an important point I would like to make. In the Outaouais region, there was an attempt recently to close three sortation centres in Hull, Gatineau and Aylmer.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out -

Order please.
The question has been put, and if the hon. member wishes to speak during the period for questions and comments, he is free to do so, but when I put the question, I did not recognize the hon. member for Hull-Aylmer.
