All right. Questions and Comments? Resuming debate. The hon. member for Hull-Aylmer.

Mr. Speaker, I heard government members criticizing the opposition, although the opposition parties have more or less agreed to let the legislation go through as soon as possible. I have no intention of delaying the process, Mr. Speaker.
However, we could start asking some serious questions about the way the government acts, especially last week, or should I say a few weeks ago, when we had to pass legislation to force public servants back to work. Today, it's the postal workers' turn, and we have to proceed with a bill to impose compulsory arbitration.
Mr. Speaker, one wonders about the irresponsible way this government handles government administration. In this respect, I would like to point out that only a few months ago, people in the Outaouais were being told that a number of sortation centres would be closed, including the centres in Aylmer, Hull and Gatineau. Thanks to the power of persuasion and the support we gave the union and the postal workers, those sortation centres remained open, Mr. Speaker, and we have every reason to be proud of the fact.
However, when the president of Canada Post receives bonuses totalling $130,000- I think it is outrageous, Mr. Speaker, to give someone who already gets a large salary a bonus for doing the government's dirty work.
Mr. Speaker, once again, I do not intend to hold up the process. I am aware that the opposition parties have agreed to shorten their speaking times so the government can get its legislation through the House. I can agree with that because after all, we cannot let a postal strike go on forever, especially when we know that Canadians and Quebecers need Canada Post.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that the way the government proceeded was totally irresponsible.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative government has struck yet another severe blow to the Atlantic provinces by slashing equalization payments.
In New Brunswick alone this Conservative policy translates into a loss of over $100 million.

Need I remind the government that equalization is a right guaranteed by the Constitution so that provincial governments can provide nearly identical public services?

The Conservative government has argued that equalization payments had not been slashed but that they were being allocated according to its funding formula. If that is the case, then I suggest that the government go back to the drawing-board and redesign this formula.
The truth is that regional disparities have risen under this government and that the economic stability of the Atlantic provinces has been undermined consistently as a result of Conservative policies.

Therefore, I urge the federal government to rethink its policies so that all Canadians can continue to have access to programs that meet national standards.

Mr. Speaker, this year is the 100th anniversary of Ukrainian immigration to Canada.
This is why they came: a country full of oppression, a village full of poverty, a household of despair.
This what they left with: a passport of desire, two arms full of farewells, many eyes full of tears, a trunk full of possessions, a heart full of faith.
This is what they experienced: a wagon full of courage, a trail of determination, two arms full of strength, many hands full of pain, many a fork full of toil, a barrel full of sweat, a rack full of patience, a truck full of sacrifice, a tub full of disappointments, a pail full of tears, an axe full of anger, a bushel of grief, a lifetime of dreams, a heart full of love, a soul full of faith.
Their contribution is colossal. Western Canada has developed and prospered due in large part to these great Canadians.
On behalf of the House of Commons may I say thank you.

Mr. Speaker, this week it has become known that Canadians will be denied the environmental and economic benefits of new clean running diesel engines which will be introduced in the United States in 1994 because Canadian refiners cannot guarantee an adequate supply of the cleaner fuel for these engines and because Canada cannot decide whether to go ahead with production of low sulphur fuel.
Instead, Canadian trucks and buses will continue to use outmoded engines which produce five times more harmful sulphur pollution. This means that Canada will be stuck with older engine technology which will not be transferable in the used vehicle market.
It means that Canadian truckers once again will find it even more difficult to compete with business south of
the border. Their vehicles will in fact be unusable in the United States. Canada does not manufacture its own diesel engines. Most diesel engines are imported from the U.S., and we will not be able to use the new engines because we cannot guarantee the fuel supply. This will cause tremendous problems to the Canadian trucking industry.
It is therefore vital that the government act immediately to ensure that Canadian truckers can survive.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I heard Pierre Pascau interview Johane Hu-rens, vice-president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, on CKVL in Montreal. During the nine-minute interview, she repeated publicly that the union would crack down and cut services to its 5,000 members who worked during the strike. Like many people, I could not believe my ears. Johane Hurens said:
-we have fines to convince people-it is a way to get back at them.
Mr. Speaker, that is reminiscent of the Dark Ages and the methods often used by organized crime, of arm twisting and the Inquisition. Nevertheless, the union will continue to collect dues which will become, I suppose, the ransom paid by these public servants who were loyal to the state and thus become the Alliance's hostages.
I therefore call upon these public servants not to be intimidated by this shameful blackmail, for serving the Canadian people is no crime. I hope that the government will not let them down; I personally promise to defend their rights here in this House and I am at their disposal.

Mr. Speaker, the symposium "Canada's Children: The Priority for the '90s" began yesterday, continues today and will end tomorrow.

October 29, 1991

Over 500 of this country's child experts are in Ottawa this week pooling their knowledge to better the lives of our children.
I salute the participants and the sponsors of this important national initiative. It addresses six areas of concern: health, welfare, poverty, families and child care, education and law.
World leaders including Canada's made a great promise a year ago to address those same concerns and thereby end child deaths and promote the well-being of children.
Today children need action to realize that great promise. I urge all colleagues to visit the child symposium, speak to the people there and learn from them.
Afterward I hope we can all come back to Parliament and work together for our children. Let us muster the political will and adopt the principle that children should be the first to benefit from our nation's success and the last to suffer from our nation's failure.
Canada's humanity and future should be tested and shaped by how Canada's Parliament protects and cares for our children: les enfants du Canada.

Mr. Speaker, addressing the 46th UN General Assembly, Cypriot President George Vasiliou stressed his government's commitment to keep striving for a just and viable solution to bring peace and security to Cyprus.
Recent UN efforts to reunite the divided island of Cyprus and settle the 17-year dispute have failed because of demands unacceptable to the UN posed by Turkey and Turkish Cypriots.
The continuing presence of Turkish troops in Cyprus has served to further exacerbate the problem.
President Vasiliou also stressed that differences must be settled by peaceful means and that democracy and strict adherence to the respect of human rights could be the basis of a solution providing for a united federal Cyprus which would demonstrate that differences could be bridged and trust repaired.
I believe the time has come for Turkey to abide by UN resolutions and get out of Cyprus. I believe as well that
the world family of nations needs to create a system of making acts of aggression no longer possible and to reverse similar situations that unfortunately still exist in the world today.

Mr. Speaker, Friday, October 25, marked the kick-off of Canadian Diabetes Week.
Currently over one million Canadians have diabetes. Every year 60,000 new cases of diabetes are diagnosed in Canada and about one in twenty Canadians can expect to develop diabetes some time in their life.
Although more people suffer from diabetes than any of the other currently non-curable diseases, the amount of money given by the federal government for research into the disease is falling behind.
We can only respond effectively to the challenges of diabetes if we understand the issues, risks and options. I believe that we as parliamentarians have a responsibility to participate in this learning process and to encourage this government to put more money into research for diabetes.
Hopefully with awareness and information the risks associated with diabetes can be reduced. Continued basic research will one day lead to a cure, but it will require a commitment from all Canadians to participate in whatever way we can to assist the Canadian Diabetes Association and the people suffering from diabetes.

Mr. Speaker, most people in my riding of Joliette, as well as in the rest of Quebec, still hope that we will find a constitutional agreement that will be beneficial and honourable for all regions of Canada. Lately, we have noted among Canadians a willingness to dialogue, perhaps for the last time.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I learned yesterday that the New Democratic member for Edmonton East stirs up passions with disturbing or ill-considered decisions, such as not inviting the French Canadian Association of Alberta to participate in his activities on the Constitution. Mr. Speaker, I want to denounce this hypocritical attitude of

October 29, 1991
the NDP, which claims to promote the building of a united and prosperous country, while at the same time not hesitating to reject outright the legitimate aspirations of Francophones in Canada. There is nothing constructive in this attitude when we are trying to build a country.

Mr. Speaker, members of this House may have heard a news story that ran this past weekend well entitled Indian Players are not Welcome in Quebec City.
A peewee hockey team from Thompson in my riding was told it could not be billeted with white families during the Quebec International Peewee Hockey Tournament because there were six native players on the team. The native players were told they must stay at a native village near Quebec City, while white players could stay with white families.
The comments made by the president of the Quebec International Peewee Hockey Tournament are alarming and insulting. He has demonstrated an abysmal lack of respect for our aboriginal peoples. He has reflected a complete misunderstanding of a modem Canada that is proud of all its peoples. His remarks are totally out of place at a time when national unity is needed now more than ever.
The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport must step in. He should investigate whether this tournament received any indirect support from the Government of Canada and he should seek an apology to native peoples from each of the team members and their families.
Oh, oh.
I really object, Mr. Speaker, to the attitude of certain Bloc members in this House on this very serious issue.

Mr. Speaker, the recent $800 million federal farm aid package was welcomed by Saskatchewan farmers. Unfortunately leaks by some members of the third line of defence committee suggest that the committee will recommend distribution of these funds on the basis of seeded acres only.
Such a method of payment is grossly unfair to tens of thousands of producers in Saskatchewan for whom summer fallow is a very necessary and sound cropping practice. The land across much of southern Saskatchewan is suitable only for cereal production and does not lend itself to diversification.
These producers are hardest hit by the ravages of the international grains trade war. I therefore urge the Minister of Agriculture to recognize the plight of farmers in southern Saskatchewan by providing a partial payment on summer fallow acreage.

Mr. Speaker, these days, Prince Charles, Princess Diana and their sons are in Canada.
I find it unacceptable that Quebecers have to foot the bill for this visit, especially after the statement made by the Prince of Wales on the Quebec question. He would be better advised to look after the problems in Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
The monarchy is an outdated, undemocratic system that we could easily do without. At a time when thousands are unemployed, on welfare and homeless in Quebec, our taxes are used to receive the royal family.

Mr. Speaker, women and children facing domestic violence need somewhere safe to go. In 1988 the government introduced Project Haven to fund the capital costs for emergency shelters. It is important for women to have somewhere to go upon leaving these short-term shelters.
October 29, 1991

I am happy to say that this government has responded to this need with a program called "The Next Step". This program focuses on the development of interim accommodation for abused women and their children. Here they are encouraged to live independently in a secure and comfortable environment, supported by the community.
Secure housing is a critical step in protecting women and children who have left abusive relationships. Congratulations on this initiative.

Mr. Speaker, within the last 24 hours the people of Tiverton, Nova Scotia have seen a storm that caused one lobster boat to sink at its moorings. The storm has driven two others ashore and pushed a fourth out into the harbour dragging its mooring.
Because of the demand for spaces fishermen have been asking for an extension to the Tiverton wharf for many years. At one time the Tiverton extension had a high priority. However, this government has no policy to extend or repair existing structures.
Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious matter, as I am sure you are aware. Replacing or repairing their boats will be expensive for these fishermen. Their lobster season could be over before it even begins, all because small craft harbours has no money to provide for adequate structures along the coast of South West Nova.
I call on the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to look into the wharf extension at Tiverton immediately and provide small craft harbours with money.

Mr. Speaker, again it is important to bring to the attention of the House that the question of funding for the Fraser River Debris Control Program has not yet been resolved and that this very valuable program is in danger of collapsing.
It is ironic that we are able to find $100 million for new projects on the Fraser but cannot find the $180,000 to
Oral Questions
maintain an existing, cost effective, valuable program that is already functioning well. Everyone using the Fraser River, such as tow boat operators, fishermen, hunters, pleasure boat operators, and all of the Fraser Valley municipalities support the continuation of this important program.
I call on the ministers of transport, fisheries, forestry and the environment to get together and resolve this problem as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, VIA Rail is currently advertising a 33 per cent off seat sale for its service between Vancouver, Kamloops and Toronto.
I applaud this measure by VIA to promote its service, but regretfully VIA has not decided to offer the same package on the Skeena route, a service between Prince Rupert, Prince George and Jasper. In fact the government has yet to decide on the future of this remote service.
VIA should promote the Skeena and offer the same seat sale on that run. The government should make up its mind and tell northern B.C. that the Skeena will be saved and promoted.
This government should take a look at the train today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. This morning, a presentation was made by two ministers, who told us things that Canadians have known very well for a long time, namely that Canada has trouble competing internationally and that we are going through a crisis.
Could the Prime Minister tell us if the government has other techniques to get us out of this crisis than to set up yet another study group that will spend money to find

October 29, 1991
Oral Questions
solutions for the government, solutions that should have been found in the last seven years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend is very well aware of the success that we have had in getting interest rates down close to 6 percentage points since the peak of last year. That is generating support for the housing industry and for automotive industry.
We are seeing now in the broader economic numbers that the strength in those industries is encouraging growth in other industries. We are making progress.
I think what is important for us as Canadians to do here-and it is the primary objective of this initiative that my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and I announced this morning-is to draw people's attention to the important challenges that we have in continuing the growth and the prosperity that we have had in the country over the last number of years.
That will be found in a greater focus and a greater understanding of the opportunities in research and development, in learning and education, in investment and in improving the performance of our domestic economy, as well as putting all that together and doing better internationally.
That is the objective of the exercise and that is what we announced this morning.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. minister would be well advised to look back to 1984 when he produced a document that was called A New Direction for Canada wherein he talked about all the same things they talked about this morning.
This morning the minister said these very enlightening phrases to the Canadian public: "We have one of the highest high school dropout rates in the world: 30 per cent compared to 2 per cent in Japan". The minister said: "We face a critical shortage of scientists and engineers". The minister said: "We rank 20 out 24 in the efficacy of our training programs". The minister said: "Canadian companies spend only one-half of what the American companies are spending on training".
This is a condemnation coming from the benches of the government.
I would like to know from the minister or the Prime Minister when we will see action after seven years of failures as admitted by the two ministers this morning.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the Opposition has referred to the agenda for economic renewal and in that we talk about the same things there as we are talking about today.
Let us look at what has happened in investment. Time and time again we hear from the hon. member about the investment encouragement that we have provided through the reduction in the change of taxation for small business, the capital gains exemption for small business, the change in FIRA to Investment Canada to encourage investment by foreigners in Canada and the research and development challenge, what we have done to lighten the load of research and development expenditures for small business through the research and development tax credit.
Under our leadership Canada has the best regime for research and development taxation privileges as any other country in the world. The productivity challenge, what we have done to-
I think we will have to move on.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the minister to talk to the 1,500,000 Canadians who are looking for jobs today. I would like him to talk to the scientific community in Canada today about research and development and he will hear something very different.
These people will be asking the minister why the government will spend another $20 million on consultants and on advertising when we need money to solve the economic problems of the nation.
When will we have that priority first and foremost?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what my hon. friend ignores totally is the fact that since 1984 Canada has had the best job creation rate of the industrialized countries.
October 29, 1991

Let us look at the bottom line and understand what is going on here. The primary objective of this exercise is to draw together a wide ranging number of points of view on how we can do better on research and development, how we can do better on learning, how we can do better on investment, how we can do better on reducing the barriers between the provinces and how we can do better internationally.
I have not heard the views of the hon. member opposite, but we are trying to get the steering group to draw together all of these views into a national consensus.

Mr. Speaker, this minister ignores reality and the reality is that this government has slashed education transfers totalling $9.5 billion over eight years. It has frozen student loans and taxed those loans for the first time in history.
Oh, oh.
Perhaps the hon. member could put his question.

Mr. Speaker, this government has taxed books and other educational materials with the GST and is spending only $4.40 per year on each illiterate person in the country.
My question is for the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister give me and any member of this House even one reason why Canadians should now believe this government when it says it is moving education to the front of the national agenda.

Mr. Speaker, I will be happy to. In the documents tabled today by the two ministers there is a very clear indication that in Canada our total educational expenditures as a percentage of GDP rank the third highest in the industrialized world.
A few years ago we were spending more money per capita than any industrialized country except Sweden, yet we were not getting the results in the areas my hon. friend raises.
High school dropouts pose a serious problem. Illiteracy is a very serious problem. Productivity growth is a very serious problem in Canada, which is why the minister is seeking to bring together labour, management, the private sector, voluntary organizations and the federal
Oral Questions
and provincial governments into one national commitment to try and get rid of illiteracy, to try and improve our productivity, thereby strengthening the national wealth of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this government has launched a $20 million trick or treat on Canadians. It is a trick on Canadians and a treat for the government's advertising and consulting friends.
Why should Canadians believe the government is seriously interested in training when the same government has cut transfers over eight years by nearly $10 billion and has penalized students with a tax on student loans.
If the government wants to spend money wisely, stop this regressive tax on student loans and do it today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all let me say to the hon. member that the numbers he is using are not correct. We have been increasing the transfers to the provinces for education.
When the hon. member uses expressions like trick or treat, let me say to him that Canadians are fed up to here with that sort of cute political phrase.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Today his government tabled two papers on competitiveness and prosperity and the need for more education, more research and development. I think most Canadians would agree that if there was a report card on this government, it would get a clear "F" on both competitiveness and prosperity.
I want to ask the Prime Minister this question. In these papers it assumes that the GST and the Canada-U.S. trade deal are the cornerstones of this government's policies. Since the introduction of the Canada-U.S. trade deal we have not had an objective assessment tabled in this House on the trade deal or the GST. Will he do that and show us objectively the results of the programs that he has put forward?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concerning the free trade agreement with

Oral Questions
the United States, since 1988, the last year before the free trade agreement came into play, our surplus with the United States-that is the excess of our exports to the United States less our imports- has gone up by $3.5 billion. We have seen our exports to the United States go up by $8 billion, or close to 8 per cent.
We have also seen in August the level of exports to the United States at an all-time high.
Surely my hon. friend cannot deny the impact of those figures. Those figures say that the bottom line performance of the Canadian economy has been positive in the area of trade since the start of the free trade agreement.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
The million and a half unemployed and those others in society who are suffering, the over one million people on social assistance, do not see those results.
Consultation is part of the presentation by the government today. There have been many very recent reports, including those by the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, the Canadian Federation of Students Strategy for Change Royal Society of Canada on the need for more research and development, Action Canada Network centre for policy alternatives, on the kind of economic and research and development policies that are needed.
I note that in the consultation process the Prime Minister and the minister are suggesting that the head of the steering committee will represent organizations funded by mostly multinational corporations.
Will the minister replace one of those co-chairs by a representative, for example, from the National Poverty Organization to show Canadians that he is really prepared to listen to all Canadians on the future agenda for Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Tbade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend is well aware of the fact that we had some other proposals in mind some weeks ago as to how we would proceed with the steering group. We offered one of the co-chairs to the Canadian Labour Congress. I am sorry that it did not see fit to participate in the steering group but I hope that we will
hear the voice of labour through a number of other ways during the course of these negotiations.
My hon. friend talks about Mr. McCamus, one of the co-chairs. Mr. McCamus was bom in Ontario. He is the president and chief executive officer of Xerox Canada. She is right there. But he was there when the first ever gold award for quality was won by that company from the Canadian government. He is the founding chairman of the Information Technology Association and is currently the chairman of the Corporate Higher Education Forum. We believe that the qualifications of Mr. McCamus, a passionate Canadian, are well suited to be the co-chair of this steering committee.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question.
What I was asking the minister was simply to make sure that the message sent to Canadians was that this government is prepared to listen to all Canadians. It would be done by putting a co-chair of that committee representing other aspects of society.
Mr. Speaker, my question deals with another topic. The Prosperity Secretariat will cost $7.5 million. For the unemployed, the homeless and the poor, this government's answer is more bureaucracy. Why should these people have confidence in this government's prosperity agenda?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not a bureaucratic exercise. This is an exercise that is designed to allow Canadians in 150 to 175 communities across Canada to feed directly into a process which will give them a say in how this country is run in the indefinite future. It will give Canadians an opportunity at the community base level to feed into a steering group which is not a government steering group, but a private sector-led steering group. It will involve people from social groups as well, so that the voices that she wants to have heard in this exercise will be heard.
I think this is a tremendous response to the concerns that Canadians have been expressing in recent years.
October 29, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I guess that is the difference between the minister's party and our party. He wants to feed into steering groups. We would like to feed Canadians.
Given that there have literally been thousands of Hamiltonians laid off in the last two years as a result of his government's economic policies, can the Prime Minister tell me what I should say to the worker at Newman Steel who received his lay-off notice last week when there is not a penny for retraining programs for him, and yet this government has $20 million to pay for a Tory boondoggle. What should I tell the laid-off worker in my riding?
Don't vote Tory.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
The hon. member should first confess to this gentleman to having fought a measure which this government tried to introduce to provide training money for laid-off workers in Canada. She should do that first.
Then she could point to the agreement that was reached between CIC, the union and the employers in the steel industry which put in place mechanisms to retrain those people and help them to find jobs so that they can earn a living. This is what the hon. member should do for a start.

Mr. Speaker, while thousands are unemployed in Montreal, Matane and the Ottawa Valley, it is unfortunate that the government can find $20 million to set up a screen to hide its own incompetence when they don't have a cent for the unemployed. Mr. Speaker, how can the government find $20 million for its Tory friends but can't find a penny for the unemployed people in Montreal? Why is that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is incredible what some people will say for partisan reasons! The hon. member should recognize that this government will spend some $3,154 billion under the Canadian Jobs Strategy precisely to help the unemployed, and workers who must adjust to the globalization of the economy.
Oral Questions
Surely the hon. member can find something in the numerous programs mentioned by Jean de Grandpre; there are 400 of them across the country. And let me tell you that the people in Matane, Montreal and Quebec know how to benefit from those programs.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the minister of industry and trade. The government's document tabled today says that the focus of the consultations the government wants to have with Canadians will not be on economic issues, like the level of the Canadian dollar, but instead will be on other issues. It says, and I quote, "by the nuts and bolts of the real economy". Why does the government not think that the level of the Canadian dollar is part of the real economy and why does the government not want to listen to Canadians for example exporters that want to tell the minister what the level of the Canadian dollar has been doing to them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not ignoring the level of the Canadian dollar. We are not ignoring some of the other policies like deficits or levels of interest rates, or anything like that.
What we have been hearing from the experts on competitiveness is that the true competitiveness of an economy is based on the way individual industries and individual people use research and development, use training, use investment, to compete in international markets.
That is what generates the competitive position of an economy. That is the focus of the consultations we are having, but that does not exclude other matters which Canadians want to bring in. We expect they will do that and we are certainly willing to listen and respond to any suggestions that are made.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister and I invite him to read the preface to his own document which sends a different message.
I ask the minister if, in what he has just said, he is not admitting, the government is not admitting, that for the

October 29, 1991
Oral Questions
past seven years they have been ignoring what they now say only now are the nuts and bolts of the real economy. What excuse does the government have to offer Canadians for this astounding failure to recognize what is important along with the dollar and interest rates in terms of jobs and well-being for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have not been ignoring the matters of learning. My colleague has talked about the substantial increase in the amount of spending that we have done since 1984 on retraining people who are losing jobs. We have not ignored the elements of research and development. We have introduced a number of policies to increase the amount of spending and increase the support for research and development.
The same can be said in trying to improve the performance of our domestic economy and also to expand our horizons to other markets, particularly through broadening our trading arrangements both with the United States and now with the multinational trade negotiations going on in Geneva.
All of these, if you look back-
I think we should move on.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has suggested that he is prepared to take seriously the messages which come from this consultation process.
Across this country 71 per cent of Canadians have indicated that they oppose the goods and services tax. I want to ask the minister if the government will follow what people tell them to do with the goods and services tax in these consultations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to my hon. friend this morning. I think we agree that we should be doing things to improve the competitive position of the Canadian economy.
I would presume that my hon. friend still agrees with that. He is not nodding because he knows that he does agree with that. The point is that the goods and services tax is designed to improve the competitive position of Canadian companies in the economy, both exporting and
competing against imports. That is precisely the reason we brought it in, because the old tax was inhibiting exports and favouring imports against Canadian production.
Surely my hon. friend must realize the impact of that and the importance of bringing the GST in to improve our competitive position.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the goods and services tax has hurt small business in every part of this country because of the competition with the United States.
If the minister does not realize that he is blind. He says that he is going to take these consultations seriously.
I ask him to answer the question and to be clear. Will this minister and this government respect what people say to this government when they speak out against the GST in these consultations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me be very clear with my hon. friend. The objective of this exercise is to find ways that we can compete more effectively as a country.
If people say that they would like something done because it is nice to do but it does not improve the competitive position of the Canadian economy then, no, we are not going to accept that.
As to suggestions and recommendations on how we improve the performance of the economy, improve our competitive position, yes, we will listen very closely to those recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, in its 1984 agenda for economic renewal the government said: "We have a clear sense of economic direction. However we do not intend to act without seeking the opinion of all
Canadians".
Today, seven lost years later, this government is still in the starting blocks. Will the government admit this prosperity document is proof of seven years of failed direction, failed commitment and failed leadership?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the seven years since we have been
October 29, 1991

in office this country has led the industrialized world in job creation.
We have been second only to Japan for a large part of that period in economic growth so how can my hon. friend say that these have been lost years? They have been years of great prosperity, but we want to ensure that we continue that prosperity.
I would suggest that my hon. friend, rather than look back and make these political points about the past, look forward to the future, look forward to how we can improve our performance in science and technology, in investment, and in research and development.

Mr. Speaker, the minister wants Canadians to forget the last seven years. His own document is testimony to his failure during that period of time.
Let me go back to the process. The minister said this morning that Canadians want to be consulted. This is the minister who would not listen to Canadian exporters and manufacturers about the level of the dollar. This is the minister who would not listen to Canadians about the GST and labour. His own document says they are one the key players in our economic future. He cannot even get labour to the table.
How can Canadians have any faith in this government or in this process?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend, the Leader of the Opposition, will recognize this quote because it is from him. He said: "We believe that market forces should continue to determine the appropriate exchange value for our currency. What we are doing as we have done consistently for the past eight years is to smooth out erratic fluctuations and the value of the dollar as they occur in the marketplace".
This is precisely the policy that this government has been following. Why does he rail away about the Canadian dollar when his leader has stated what the policy is and continues to be.
I just say to my hon. friend one more time: what we are looking for here is a productive debate on how we can put a firm underpinning under our standard of living. We
Oral Questions
are starting from a position of strength. We have the second highest standard of living in the world. We are number five in competitive position, but there are those danger signs on the horizon that are clearly set out in these documents.
What we want to achieve is a consensus, drawing on the ideas of the hon. member as well as all Canadians, on how we can improve our performance.

Mr. Speaker, I have in my possession a stack of reports that have been issued over the last five years by people like the Science Council, the Economic Council of Canada, Senate committees, House committees, task forces and working groups.
My question to the government is this. The reports all deal with the same questions that are in the documents issued this morning.
Has the government not read any of these reports, or does it dismiss all the answers contained in all these reports already prepared at taxpayers' expense? What is going on here? Why is there $20 million for yet another investigation of the same questions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been reports, a wide range of reports. My hon. friend has referred to some; the Leader of the New Democratic Party has referred to others. But there are differences in points of view. Might I suggest that there are even differences in points of view among my hon. friend and the member for Windsor West and the member for Winnipeg South West. There are differences within his own party.
We are trying on a national basis to reconcile those differences through this broad consultation process, drawing on experts in the field, in the steering group that will be bringing forward a national action plan with recommendations for the federal government, provincial governments, territorial governments, municipal governments and the private sector in all its capacities.

Mr. Speaker, what we are looking for from this government maybe is a point of view. There is nothing in this document that expresses any opinions about what direction the country should be going to solve its underlying problems.

October 29, 1991
Oral Questions
Now that $20 million is on the table, what has happened to all these old reports? Is there nothing in them? Was that money wasted or is the new money wasted?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the member will see in some of those reports that they recommended the goods and services tax. They recommended the free trade agreement with the United States. The Macdonald commission on the economy-
More, more.
Why didn't you agree with that?

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: For the hon. member to say that we are not listening to these reports or for my friend over here from Willowdale to say "act", we have acted but we also feel it is a good time to reflect on this range of reports, draw out a national consensus for a national action plan that we can all get behind as a country and in that way move on to greater heights across the country.

Mr. Speaker, although the energy efficiency bill given first reading this morning allows the Governor in Council to prescribe fuel efficiency standards for internal combustion engine vehicles-the greatest source of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in Canada-the government apparently intends for the time being to set standards only for household electric appliances. In other words, they will regulate toasters but not trucks, tea kettles but not Cadillacs.
My question is for the minister of energy. When will the government prescribe internal combustion engine vehicles and set efficiency standards for them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the latter point, as the Minister of the Environment also pointed out, we have already done that. We are going to look at further CAFE standards in terms of the auto industry.
I also refer, for example, to reports even today that the government apparently has made a decision on high sulphur diesel which is also not the case.
I say to the hon. member: thank you for supporting the energy efficiency bill as it goes. I want to discuss with him even further what other action we should take together.

Mr. Speaker, given this government's record since I got here in 1988,1 would be happy to discuss any action.
Will the government at least take the simple action of proclaiming the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumptions Standards Act passed by this House in 1982 and use it to set standards at least as stringent as those slated for introduction in the United States for motor vehicles?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept to some degree what the hon. member said in the question he just asked, that there has to be some co-ordination, some synergy, because of an integrated auto and truck market and production in the United States and Canada. We should be very close, if not lock-step, to those regulations in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this note I would like to take a moment to extend my thanks to the two House leaders opposite and to the chairman of the standing committee, the hon. member for Portage-Interlake, for agreeing to refer this bill for pre-study. I would also like to thank the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations for its excellent work.
I would like especially to express my personal thanks, as I said, to the hon. member for Dartmouth and the hon. member for Nickel Belt. From the day that Bill C-22 was first introduced it was clear that their participation would be well informed and constructive. The contributions they have made demonstrate that they recognize the urgency of the passage of this bill so as to better protect the interests of Canadians within a competitive marketplace.
Mr. Speaker, I know that the wonderful unanimity of members on both sides of the House concerning the need to proceed with the reform will sound even sweeter. We not only can but must amend this archaic law to better protect our workers, to help those who unfortunately go bankrupt recover as soon as possible and to ensure that our businesses have the modern tools
Government Orders
they need to meet the challenge of international competition.
Mr. Speaker, the real reason for our reform is to preserve jobs and promote economic growth. In the latest Speech from the Throne, our government promised to devote much of its energy during this session of Parliament to preparing the necessary ingredients for our future prosperity. We said that we would proceed in several areas: establishing clear, realistic deficit-reduction objectives; implementing the GST; exercising strict spending control; making continuing education the rule rather than the exception; and consulting our fellow citizens on ways to reduce obstacles to sustained growth and international competitiveness.
A crucial step in reaching this ambitious objective is to review our main pieces of framework legislation to ensure that their provisions help rather than hinder natural market forces, for the greater good of our fellow Canadians, Mr. Speaker.
That is the context within which our reform project is to be seen-as an essential part of the economic support structure and a major step to sustained economic growth.

I will not focus on the specifics of the legislation as I know members from all sides of the House are already familiar with them. I would like to speak about the principles that underlie them and I would like to begin by quoting the member for Dartmouth who earlier this year referred to the reform package provisions regarding stay of proceedings as especially timely. He said:
It is absolutely essential that this type of protection, which they have had in the United States for a number of years, is introduced to a modem bankruptcy act in Canada.
As we all know, because we have constituents who are in business, all too often secured creditors walk in quickly, seize assets, cut off credit lines, and put receivers in place. Many times healthy companies that, for whatever reason-they may be having some temporary difficulty-find themselves in a position where they cannot go on with their business and bankruptcy ensues.
This from June 19 Hansard at page 2108. This is precisely the reason we are proposing that the current rules be changed to provide potentially viable businesses in financial trouble with the option of filing a notice of stay with the official receiver for protection from all creditors. It is also why we are adding a new Part XI to the act, to impose duties of disclosure and good faith on secured creditors and receivers and to require that a

Government Orders
secured creditor give a debtor notice before enforcing its security.
In short we are seeking to put in dealing with the Bankruptcy Act emphasis on rehabilitation, not on liquidation. The reasons for this I think are obvious.

Mr. Speaker, bankruptcies always involve heavy costs-social and human costs that can be highly destructive. Workers lose their livelihood and too often hard-won skills. Creditors and suppliers lose money; our communities lose businesses; our entrepreneurs lose their investments and often their dreams. Mr. Speaker, these costs undermine our country's efforts to remain competitive internationally.
It is therefore absolutely crucial to have this proposed reform adopted as soon as possible. As parliamentarians, we have a responsibility to do everything we can to protect our viable businesses and especially the jobs they provide, Mr. Speaker. We can no longer afford to waste our precious resources through bankruptcies that could have been avoided.
This desire to end the shameful waste of precious resources is also behind our decision to improve protection for unpaid suppliers. For many small businesses, the loss of a single delivery might be enough to put their viability at risk, causing a chain reaction or a domino effect, if you like. Since the primary objective of the proposed reform is to reduce business bankruptcies and safeguard jobs, clearly we must provide better protection for unpaid suppliers.
Mr. Speaker, the kind of protection we propose exists, and it is effective. In fact, similar protection has been provided in Quebec for several years, to the apparent satisfaction of businesses in that province. This probably explains why associations representing small businesses in this country strongly support this proposal.

Our desire to make the Bankruptcy Act fairer also led us to amend the provisions pertaining to Crown priority, the system whereby governments are automatically assigned preferred creditor status for all moneys owed to them.
With the exception of income tax deducted at source, contributions to the Canada Pension Plan and unemployment insurance premiums, Crown priority is being reduced under the new legislation. This is because we believe rules that are perceived to be unfair or arbitrary damage the entrepreneurial spirit. It was unfair to have one set of rules in place for one category of creditors, the Crown, and not others. We have acted to remove this inequity.
In much the same way as we aimed to make the existing regime fairer and more accessible to business, we aimed to make it fairer and more accessible to consumers. The consumer provisions we are proposing, that provide individuals in financial difficulty with more breathing space in which to reorganize their affairs, are long awaited ones. So too are the provisions that will allow a debtor to negotiate with creditors to pay less than the total amount of the debt owing and to reschedule their debt payment plans over a longer period of time.
Faced with the alternative of forcing the debtor into personal bankruptcy and likely not seeing any compensation at all, most creditors will prefer to receive some amount on the dollar. Should personal bankruptcy become the only option for the unfortunate debtor, our proposals will provide for easier access to affordable and expedient administrative procedures. Both measures will make it easier for bankrupt individuals to get back on their feet and start participating fully in the economy once more.

Mr. Speaker, I could go on at length about the merits of each of the more technical amendments we are proposing, but I would like to take a few minutes to explain why we are proposing a wage claim benefits program and why I am particularly proud of being the initiator of this proposal.
Mr. Speaker, all members of this House who are more or less aware of that aspect of our reform know there were at least six attempts during the past fifteen years to update our Bankruptcy Act, and that all these attempts experienced the same fate. They died on the Order Paper. This poor record is partly due to a failure to strike the necessary balance between the legitimate rights of creditors and debtors, but also and especially to an inability to deal with the question of employee protection. That is why, when I took over, I promised myself I
October 29, 1991

Government Orders
would put an end to this string of failures. Reforms in this crucial area were too long to come about for lack of consensus on the type of protection and the means of financing that protection.
Mr. Speaker, it is a real pity and, quite frankly, I find unacceptable the fact that while we have been discussing principles and possible solutions for years, our workers are left out in the cold with little or no protection.
Great hardship was suffered by innocent bystanders to wait any longer for an illusive consensus to emerge. In fact, it is absolutely unthinkable that, in developing our proposals for change, we would take the easy way out and turn our backs on our poor wage-earners.
Not only was I firmly determined to put in place a protection plan for employees, but also to make it work efficiently.
One of the reasons why I personally carried such extensive consultations over the past few months was to see for myself how far we could and should go with our program. The program we are putting forward fully meets the real concerns of the people and the organizations we approached.
What we are proposing is accessible and easy to use. It is intended to provide a safety net to ensure that workers get the wages owed to them should their employer goes bankrupt and that they get it as quickly as possible.
By collecting the employers' contribution at the same time as their unemployment insurance premiums, we minimize administrative costs as well as their amount of paperwork.
Mr. Speaker, concerns were expressed recently about our wage claim payment plan. I wish to respond to a number of these concerns, because I think it is important that our fellow citizens have a clear picture of what our program is and what it is not.
First, judging by the nature and tone of some speeches, it is obvious that there is confusion, misunderstanding, about the raison d'etre of our program. This program is, first and foremost, one in a series of steps aimed at updating our antiquated Bankruptcy Act and the basic idea is to keep viable businesses afloat, protect jobs and realign the rights of both creditors and debtors.

The program is not intended as a mechanism for income substitution or as a means of providing general compensation to workers for job losses resulting from a bankruptcy. Rather, it is a safety net that has been designed to ensure that individuals owed moneys by their bankrupt employers for wages or expenses receive an acceptable level of protection.
Second, some groups have argued that a simpler way of dealing with the issue of moneys owed to employees of a bankrupt firm would be to give them super priority over other creditors.
This approach to wage earner protection was proposed in earlier attempts to amend the Bankruptcy Act and was rejected every time by all even here in the House and by other stakeholders outside in the Landry committee and the Colter committee.
Why? For one thing it is neither sure nor prompt. It takes time to liquidate the assets of a bankrupt firm when and if there are any assets to liquidate. Super priority wage earners would be forced to wait several months before finding out whether they would be receiving wages owed to them.
Third, it is important to note that the wage claim protection program will be funded through an employer contribution of roughly 10 cents per week per employee. Money thus collected will be earmarked specifically for this program. For this reason the program cannot be used as a so-called cash cow to raise revenues for other purposes. I believe the following examples help to put this tax in its proper perspective.
For the average sized Canadian business employing 15 people it would mean $1.50 per week, the equivalent of the price of a large bag of potato chips. For the average small and medium sized business employing an average of seven people, 10 cents per employee per week means 70 cents a week, which is less than the price of a cup of coffee.

Mr. Speaker, some have suggested that such an additional burden could jeopardize the competitiveness of our companies on world markets.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth. Moreover, whereas the level of the tax or contribution is minimal, the benefits of the program for workers and for businesses as well will be very significant.
Some say that the maximum authorized payment is too low. Mr. Speaker, it would have been easy to be generous with other people's money. However, the objective of this program is to provide workers with an acceptable level of protection for the money owed them. The $2,000 maximum payment provided by the program is equivalent to about twice the amount owed to employees caught in bankruptcies and should be more than enough to cover the vast majority of salary claims, according to studies that we have on hand.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, nothing will prevent an individual owed more than $2,000 from claiming the excess as an ordinary debt. Some have suggested that we should finance the program through the general revenues of the government. This suggestion simply cannot be implemented, given our huge deficit at the present time.
I would now like to take a few moments to discuss the report of the Standing Committee on the preliminary study of Bill C-22. This report is indeed eloquent testimony to the usefulness of a pre-study. In my opinion, it demonstrates clearly that the process is valid and constructive.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I must thank all the members of the Committee. The spirit of cooperation that prevailed enabled us to make great progress. In fact, the most remarkable thing about the hearings held during the pre-study is that, while each group that appeared before the Committee endeavoured, as one would expect, to protect its own interests in the context of the reform, a strong and genuine consensus emerged from those hearings regarding the reform proposals as a whole, and a very clear message was sent to the lawmakers: What are you waiting for to support this reform?
Following this detailed study, the Committee released a report in which it recommends several amendments to the bill. After carefully examining the Committee's report, and consulting with experts from my department and outside, I am pleased to announce in this House that
we will accept most of the recommendations made by the Committee. These excellent recommendations which deal, among other things, with commercial reorganization and winding-up arrangements, will significantly improve the reform of the Bankruptcy Act.
Unfortunately, some recommendations are unacceptable to us. The government and the opposition critics have agreed-and I want to thank my two colleagues, whom I met last week-that it was impossible to reach an agreement on two issues, namely the absolute priority of salary claims and the rights of unpaid suppliers. However, our accepting most of the Committee's recommendations demonstrates the good faith shown by both sides of the House.
In any case, the three parties agreed that Bill C-22 is reasonable and balanced, and a most adequate answer to the pressing needs of a modem and dynamic economy.
Over the past months I have made a point of consulting closely with my provincial counterparts to ensure our regime meshes smoothly with existing or planned provincial ones.
I am pleased to report that we are proceeding satisfactorily. The new proposed bankruptcy and insolvency act offers flexible, modem rales that recognize natural market forces. It is an important element of the framework that will allow this government to foster a competitive productive national economy.
This bill provides clear and vital benefits for Canadian businesses, workers and consumers. The passage of Bill C-22 will create a smoother operating and fairer bankruptcy and insolvency system in this country.
On the other hand, I do not even want to think about the consequences of delaying or halting the progress of this legislation. We in this House have the power to pass laws that make our legal system better, laws that encourage prosperity and growth, laws that help Canadians.
We have such an opportunity before us. It is my fervent hope that this important piece of legislation will be passed without delay by Parliament so that we may replace the existing law and end the 40 years of drought.
October 29, 1991



Mr. Speaker, I was heckled earlier, at the beginning of my speech, by members who criticized me. I am sorry to see that they are gone now as for the most part of my speech. It is easy for the Bloc Quebecois to criticize, but when the time comes to listen and find out how a bill can serve the interests of all Canadians, including the people of Quebec, they disappear from the surface of the earth. That is what happens, Mr. Speaker. They only want to impress the media.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move the following:
That Bill C-22, An Act to enact the Wage Claim Payment Act, to
amend the Bankruptcy Act and to amend other Acts in consequence
thereof, not be referred to Legislative Committee G but rather to the
