Mr. Speaker, I rise today to join my colleague, the minister, in debate on this very important piece of infrastructural legislation concerning the marketplace of our country: Bill C-22, an act to amend the Bankruptcy Act, an act to enact the Wage Claim Payment Act and other particular technical amendments.
We have just gone through a fairly new procedure from all sides of this House. After this bill was initially put to the House for first reading back about June 12 all sides of the House agreed, in the interests of trying to provide for better legislative process, to have it referred to the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
The reason that we did that is that there was a recognition on all sides of this House that the area of bankruptcy and bankruptcy reform had to be a priority
Government Orders
with the government and with members of all sides of this House.
Rather than wait until second reading debate when we all get up and have our say about the principles that are enshrined in this particular piece of legislation, in order not to unduly hold up the process, all sides agreed to do basically a pre-study after first reading.
Before I get into the substantive part of my remarks on the various aspects of this legislation I want to state clearly up front that the process which we have just gone through, my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, my colleagues in the Liberal Party and in the Conservative Party, of allowing members prior to approval of the bill in principle at second reading to sit down and debate a piece of legislation as if it were draft legislation has been an extremely productive and positive experience for all of us.
What we saw was a departure from the normal cut and thrust of partisanship which normally happens after second reading when a bill goes to committee. We did not see in most cases, and I underline most because it was not in all cases, government members digging their heels in and indicating that no matter what was raised by other members of the committee, it certainly could not be correct because it was contrary to what the minister or what the department had put forward in the bill.
All of the members who were interested came back two weeks early and heard witnesses from various interest groups across the country. Interestingly enough, at the end of the process we came up with a near consensus. I think there was one member of the committee who did not agree in the report that was placed after the pre-study.
We came up with a consensus about the types of things we wanted to see reformed this bill and to bring in better legislation. I am going to refer to some of those recommendations as I go along in my presentation today.
I want to say at the outset that this is exactly the type of process that should be looked at by all sides of this House because it truly is a way to involve members on the government backbenches and members of the opposition, be they Liberals, New Democrats, or independents, in a very positive way in the legislative process.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
I understand the government is not going to accept all of the 22 or so amendments that were put forward. The government has indicated that it is prepared to accept a majority of the recommendations before this bill receives final approval in the House of Commons.
That has to be something that is very positive and must be underlined for all Canadians who all too often, but for good reason, see most of what we do here as pretty much irrelevant and see the role of the private member as less than irrelevant at the best of times.
I want to commend the minister and the two House leaders for embarking us on this trek into the unknown when we did pre-study after first reading. It truly is one of the ways that this place can reform the way it does its business and to put some respect back into the parliamentary process and put respect back into the job of being a parliamentarian.
It has been a long time since bankruptcy legislation has come before this House. The current bill was enacted in 1949. It was slightly amended in 1966, but not substantially amended. Since then the minister has indicated in his speech that there were were six attempts before the Parliament of Canada to tiy and reform that particular piece of legislation.
In actual fact there have been at least nine attempts, or perhaps 10, six of which were through legislation, either legislation introduced in the Senate or legislation that eventually died on the Order Paper in this place.
In each and every case there were certain objectives put forward when we were looking at reform of bankruptcy legislation. I want to paraphrase Coulter because it seems to be one of the recent authorities on what we should be looking for in bankruptcy reform legislation.
Coulter said that first, bankruptcy legislation reform should be fair and equitable. Second, it should establish a proper equilibrium in the balance of power between the debtor, the secured creditor, and the unsecured creditor. Third, bankruptcy legislation should allow for effective reorganization and support the maintenance of viable business enterprise. Fifth, it should be flexible. Sixth, the legislation should recognize the special circumstances of different categories of debtors.
He used as an example farmers and fishermen.
We have had a long time between drinks at the well. It has been a long time since this bankruptcy legislation has been put forward for much-needed reform.
I should say at this particular juncture that the bill before us, Bill C-22, sets out in a fairly categorized way to address eight concerns that have been raised through countless consultations and countless studies and countless bills that have been put before us. There are some which we are not approaching today which Coulter had mentioned and they are farmers, fishermen and international insolvencies and perhaps one or two other things. This bill is broken down basically into eight sections: wage earner protection, and I am going to spend most of my time on that today, commercial reorganizations, consumer proposals, consumer bankruptcy, secured creditors and receivers, Crown claims and priorities, protection of unpaid suppliers, and a whole host of technical amendments.
This is not an appropriate time for us to be dealing with bankruptcy reform legislation. I would like to have seen it a little earlier. I am sure the minister would like to have as well. I cannot help but wonder why the bankruptcy legislation that is before us comes after a very deep and veiy severe recession.
One of the key points in the bill is the wage earner protection fund which seeks to try to re-establish some balance, as Coulter said, between the rights of various creditors. It is interesting to note that as we talk about bankruptcies we find our economy continuing in a state of decline.
Since 1984 there have been in excess of 273,000 bankruptcies. The assets of those 273,000 bankruptcies are in excess of $20 billion. During that period nearly
3,000	farmers have gone bankrupt. That is a lot of farms out of production. That is a lot of farm families getting a lot of farm stress and it is a heck of a lot of pain for those individuals.
Anyone who knows anything about farming will tell you for every farmer who goes bankrupt there is probably another 10 who are insolvent but there is no sense in the bank foreclosing because it cannot do anything with the assets. Truly it is the tip of the iceberg.
October 29, 1991

Regarding fishermen, 3,102 fishermen have had to declare bankruptcy between 1984 and the September statistics that were put out just Friday by Statistics Canada. People ask: "You're dealing with bankruptcy reform, Ron, what do you think is the cause of this accelerated rate of bankruptcies?"
It is clear, the accelerated rate of bankruptcies is caused by the three pillars of this government's economic policies, one of which is the high dollar policy. I looked in the paper today and I think the dollar is at 88 cents. Anyone who knows anything about our export based industries knows that for every cent that the dollar goes up, there is about $1.4 billion lost in Canadian exports. Over the last year when we have seen the Canadian dollar go to those almost all-time highs, at least in the last dozen years, some analyses said that we have lost as much as $143 billion in Canadian exports.
We have had a high tax policy. Thirty-two times since 1984 taxes have been raised. The GST has taken a tremendous bite out of the wallets of consumers. It has caused the collapse of consumer confidence which in turn has caused consumers to stop buying. When consumers stop buying, businesses file for bankruptcy, people lose their jobs and the economy goes into a nosedive. Thirty-two times taxes have gone up.
There was a report out just last week which said that if you took out the effect on inflation of government policies, and that is its tax policy and its high interest rate policy, when you put your equation together regarding the inflation rate you would find out that over the last 12 months Canadian businesses have done their part. There have been no increases in consumer prices other than those increases that have been the direct result of the high dollar, high interest rate policy by this government.
We see that the inflation which has caused high interest rates, the third pillar of the government's economic policy, as the Governor of the Bank of Canada will tell you, have to be imposed because we have to get inflation down.
If the Conference Board of Canada's figures which I just quoted about price increases are correct then the government's own policies have caused the dollar to rise. The government's own policies of high tax have caused inflation to rise. As a result of those first two things, the
Government Orders
government's first two policies have caused an incredibly high interest rate policy. This has led tens of thousands of Canadians and Canadian businesses over the brink into bankruptcy. Those are the facts. I raise them because in the last 12 months this economy has been beaten to death by this government's policies. There have been tens of thousands, perhaps hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers who have lost their jobs in this recession.
Since we have had so many years between drinks at the well, why is it that it is only after 100,000 Canadians have lost their jobs and after 56,000 Canadian individuals and businesses have gone bankrupt that we actually get bankruptcy reform legislation before us?
One of the pillars of the bankruptcy reform legislation is the wage earner protection fund. It has been used as the carrot on the stick. Everyone in this House I would suspect who is a caring and thinking individual recognizes that there is a great imbalance in the bankruptcy legislation. The imbalance is this. In 1949, the bill provided for up to $500 for payment of outstanding wage claims on bankrupt firms. It was not as a super priority, it was as an ordinary creditor. Status was applied to those wages. In actual fact what it meant, all through that period of time, was that by the time the assets had been disposed of, there was really nothing left for the poor worker.
Surely if we seek to fundamentally rebalance an unbalanced bill then we should sit down and look at whose interest we are serving. The government proposes in this legislation to create a new fund called the wage earner protection fund because it recognizes that there is an interest in the assets of a bankrupt or insolvent firm. There is an interest there by the employees who have not had their wages paid. It recognizes that and I applaud it for it and I recognize and support that as well.
Rather than go in and put that balance that I referred to earlier that Coulter had spoken about, in the bill, it has chosen the easier route. The easier route is: No, do not go in and try to rebalance the bill because there are a lot of very special interests out there who squeak like crazy every time you even talk about offering their position under current bankruptcy legislation. I refer to a lot of the financial institutions.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
Rather than go in and bear the wrath of the heavy lobby from the financial institutions because we are going in to try to put fairness and equity back into our bankruptcy legislation, the thing to do perhaps is to go forward and say we recognize it, but we are going to pay it out in a different way. That is what the government has proposed.
The government has come in and said: "We are going to have a wage earner protection fund". What does that mean? The proposal in Bill C-22 is that employees who are owed wages in bankrupt or insolvent firms will be able to claim for 90 per cent of the wages owed, up to a maximum of $2,000. The government is doing that because it believes in order to put a fund together it has to make sure that it is not so costly that it cannot be financed easily. So how will it finance it? Well, in the minister's own words, and he recognizes what it is, it will implement a new tax. I just said that there were 32 tax increases since 1984. Strike for 33 plus the paper burden.
Now what we have is a new tax proposed to fund an inequity that everybody believes is there in the wage earner protection fund and it truly is there. Rather than go against the banks, rather than go against the other big special interests who have been protected year after year after year by no offering of the current bankruptcy legislation, let us create a fund, a social program in effect. It will do what we really cannot find the wherewithal to do and that is truly rebalance the bill. There will be another tax and the tax is going to go in. I know it is not a lot of money. I asked the witnesses who came and they all said: "We hate this tax", and we know that it is only a few pennies. The minister mentioned it is not very much money, but Canadian businesses have been smothered with new taxes. They have been absolutely smothered by the paperwork burden imposed upon them by federal, provincial and municipal governments, all trying to take a share of that diminished profit that they have worked so hard in their businesses to create. They have had enough.
Every single witness who came forward said: "We agree that there has to be a rebalancing. We agree somebody has to pay for it. We know that. But please do not put in a new tax. We do not trust the current
provincial governments and we certainly do not trust our federal government. A tax that is $5 or $10 per employee this year will be $15, $50 or $75 in future years".
No matter how much the government protests that will not happen, we constantly get examples, such as unemployment insurance premiums.
Up 24 per cent.

They went up 24 per cent last year. It is not good. They are taking money out of small business. They are crippling small business with additional taxes.
We in the Liberal party agree there has to be something done. The wage earner protection fund, by the government's own admission, is going to tax every employer in the country. It is going to tax hospitals which find that the money made available to them from the EPF is diminishing every year because of a freeze on EPF. Hospitals do not go bankrupt in Canada, but they are going to be taxed. Their diminishing health care dollar is going to be siphoned back up from a new tax that their employees will never get to benefit from as long as they are employees of a hospital because hospitals do not go bankrupt.
It is the same with school boards and municipalities. In a very difficult economic time the government proposes to fix what we all agree is something that has to be fixed but it is doing it the wrong way, in the opinion of the Liberal Party.
We have proposed through a pre-study of this bill that we do it a different way. We dare to go in and challenge some of what has been told to us by some of those very special interest groups in the country, primarily the banks.
We said to the banks: "We have to fix this. It is not right". There are three inputs into a business. There is the entrepreneurial spirit and whatever moneys the entrepreneur has, plus all of the hard work and ingenuity needed to get a business going. That is an input.
Then there is the investor, usually a bank. It is usually a bank that comes in and makes its assessment on all of the various factors, the market, the product and the skills that are brought forward by the owner and the operator. It makes an investment of money because it thinks it will make money on the entrepreneurial spirit of the owner.
October 29, 1991

Then there is a third input as well. That third input is the labour of the employees who put their time and effort for pay into producing a product or a service.
If we really want to rebalance the bankruptcy legislation, let us do more than recognize that they have an interest. Let us put the interest in the bill.
The Liberal Party said there was no need to create a $60 million fund. That is what the government said this was going to cost. There is no need to create another tax. There is no need to create more paperwork burden.
What we can do is go in and fix the act. When we said that to the bankers, they said: "I will tell you what. If you go in and touch our interest or our secured interest", because Canadian banks are not risk takers. They tell you that up front. The most protected banking institutions in the world are Canadian banks. They told us right to our face that they are not risk takers.
Including FBDB.

Including FBDB. They are not risk takers.
What the bank said is: "If you touch our secured interest, if you put a super priority to fund those wages, it takes away from our interest and we promise you there will be a credit crunch like you never saw in this country. And in some businesses that are labour intensive, we will not be able to lend them money any more. If you touch our interest, we can go elsewhere and make our money". And I say: "Sure, we certainly believe that, Mr. Banker".
I asked the minister's staff and the departmental staff about the new Crown priority that was established about a dozen years ago, a deemed trust situation with source deductions.
know it is a much smaller amount of money. The banks argued the same case at that point. If a super priority was given to the government's claims for source deductions, it would give them a credit crunch and they would not be able to lend money. Do you know what, Mr. Speaker? The day after that particular provision was enacted in law, and there was a super priority on Crown claims, life went on. The banks continued to lend their money and businesses continued to expand and flourish, and there was no credit crunch.
So I don't believe it for a minute. You look at the system in the United States where the banks do not have
Government Orders
such a security interest in business and that is a flourishing free market economy. So don't come and tell me, protected conservative Canadian banks, that it we alter anything as far as your security interests in the assets of a company that you are not going to give them money. I say to the banks that you will adjust to whatever the regulations and the legislation is, and you will adjust like you have done in every other circumstance. You will continue to lend and you will continue to make record profits in Canada because of the other regulations and the other laws that protect Canadian banks and financial institutions.
You know, it is interesting, we are dealing with about $62 million, that is all, $62 million. There are hundreds of billions of dollars in investments made by Canadian banks. We are talking about wage claims of about $62 million. How in the name of goodness can $62 million put that very solid Canadian banking institution on its ears? It is not going to happen.
We in the Liberal party are absolutely opposed to a wage earner protection fund which is financed by a new tax on businesses and on average Canadians. We are opposed to it 100 per cent.
Through the committee process we were able to convince, between my NDP colleague from Nickel Belt and myself, all but one committee member. We were able to convince Conservative members on the other side that a new tax was the wrong way to go. We said to listen to the CFIB. There are other ways to do this. We can dare to be bold and to be innovative and we can achieve those goals that the minister set out, which is to give wage protection to employees, but we can do it in a different way. We all agreed on the goals, we just disagree on how we get there.
The Liberal party has been clear. The committee pre-studying it has been extremely clear. We don't buy the arguments from the big banks and the vested interests in this country that if we touch their security interest the entire economy is going to collapse in this country. We simply do not buy it and we will not support another tax on small business. We will not support amending a bankruptcy act, leaving almost undisturbed the unfair interest and the unbalanced interest of most of Canada's financial institutions in the assets of a bankrupt's estate.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
I have to tell you this, Mr. Speaker. This is a little interesting. It is not just Liberals and New Democrats who seek fairness. I think there are a lot of Conservatives who do as well. I have a list here of some Conservative members who filled out a questionnaire concerning whether or not they were in favour of an employer-financed wage earner protection fund, as proposed in Bill C-22. There were about 50 members of Parliament who responded, and out of that there were a number of Conservative members. The member for Athabasca said he was opposed; the member for Calgary Southeast said he was opposed; the member for Brama-lea-Gore-Malton said he was opposed; the member for Red Deer said he was opposed; the member for Lethbridge said he was opposed; the member for Bruce-Grey said he was opposed; the member for Halton-Peel said he was opposed; and the member for Edmonton Southwest, who happens to be the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who is sponsoring this bill which will impose a new tax, said at that time in the summer, that he as well was opposed to the bill.
Shame on Edmonton Southwest.

The Conservative members on the pre-study committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs as well said that they were opposed to the establishment of a new tax in order to achieve these goals. The committee report went into some length about a system that we thought would work, that would still give immediacy of payment and certainty of payment to those wage earners. We also thought that the dollar value should go from $2,000 to $3,000. We thought that the Superintendent of Bankruptcies should guarantee any loans made by a trustee to fulfill that wage earner super priority. We even said, so that it doesn't cost taxpayers a lot more money, let the trustee at the superintendent's office adjust the fees to create a fund. If a trustee has to borrow against the assets of the firm to pay out the claims of those wage earners so there is immediacy of payment, if there is any shortfall, the superintendent's office could guarantee it.
We gave them a way to do it and we hear that the government has said no.
More taxes.

More taxes, more taxes, more taxes.
There are other aspects of the bill such as commercial reorganization. This bill has a very good provision in it for commercial reorganization. We all agree that it is absolutely necessary to put some order in a very cannibalistic process at this point in dealing with commercial reorganization.
Currently under the Bankruptcy Act there really is no provision for a debtor or a company that is in debt to stop a creditor from basically jumping the queue and immediately appointing a receiver with 10 or 15 days' notice, in effect putting the company out of business. This bill seeks to rebalance that and we support this particular section of the bill wholeheartedly.
There were a number of amendments we were seeking through committee and I have discussed the matter with the minister. Some of them are technical and some are not that technical. We want to make sure, if we are going to go in and try to rescue businesses by allowing provisions for commercial reorganization, that at the same time we are not passing a piece of legislation which may be technically flawed or perhaps has not gone far enough so that the goals as outlined by the government in the proposals on reorganization can truly be obtained.
In brief, the commercial reorganization allows for a debtor to file a notice of intent. Once a notice of intent is signed, secured and unsecured creditors are stayed. They cannot do anything. They cannot jump in if they have a lien on a particular aspect of the business. They cannot jump in and stop the company from doing business. That means the business or the individual has a period of time to sit down without a gun at his or her head to try and work out a proposal with all of the creditors.
If the business has loans of a million dollars and it is only worth $700,000 and it can carry that debt, then the owner/operator along with the trustee or the receiver can sit down and work out with the creditors a more equitable arrangement so that instead of just going in and cannibalizing the assets of a firm in some financial difficulty and putting people out of work and destroying the lives of those owner/operators who would otherwise be forced into bankruptcy, it gives them some hope that there is another and better way to do it. Maybe through restructuring, through a 30-day, a 45-day or up to a six-month provision, we are giving them time to make businesses work instead of allowing the old legislation to
October 29, 1991

go on which simply put businesses out of business, many of which were very viable.
The current bill says that you can go as long as six months. This is one of the things we were looking for, but we do not think it is long enough. We have heard from a lot of our colleagues about cases like Algoma Steel in which it is going to take a long time if you are going to restructure its debt in order to save the company and thousands of jobs. We have put some recommendations forward through the committee. It is my hope that the government will be looking at those recommendations.
There is also some very good news dealing with revindication. We finally recognize that there is an interest in the assets of a bankrupt firm that has to take a super priority and that is the interest of those suppliers that have supplied goods to a company that suddenly goes bankrupt. We live on credit. Nobody pays cash these days. All too often we have heard, and the government has heard in the past, that suppliers of goods supply goods to a company and if the company knows it is in financial difficulty oftentimes it will stock up on stock, get rid of the stock at ridiculously low prices to try to stave off secured creditors like banks, or if they know the company is going to be going under they will stock up on the stock. The company is petitioned into bankruptcy and those individuals have no preferred claim on their own goods in the store or retail outlet that are unaltered, that are still identifiable, because the receiver will come in and liquidate the assets of the company.
This bill seeks to remedy that situation by giving revindication rights for those goods and services that are unaltered, are identifiable and in the same form. That is a very positive step. There are some problems with it and the problems have been addressed in the committee report. I met with the minister last week to look at trying to fix it a little bit.
I mentioned earlier that we can get stays of proceedings of 10 days, 21 days and extended each time after that by 45 days, in which case nobody can take any actions against a firm that is under protection. There is a problem here because as I have indicated you have just given a 30-day provision to a supplier of goods to revindicate. We have indicated in a report what should be done. I might sell goods to a company and then 10
Government Orders
days after I sell the goods to the company it might apply for protection under the proposed act. My clock continues to tick. Maybe 21 days later when I am one day over my 30 days that I could revindicate, the company is unable to come to an agreement with its creditors, goes bankrupt and as for my interest in the stock it has on hand, which is unpaid for, I have lost my ability to revindicate.
We have made provisions and we have made recommendations to the minister that in cases such as that the 30-day clock should cease. It should be held so that when a company goes in and applies for 10 days' protection or it goes up to 31 days' protection, the revindication clock for the supplier also has a stay during that period of time so that at the end of the period, if there is no reorganization and its goods are still there in an unaltered form, it can still go in and revindicate.
We have also found some technical problems with the particular piece of legislation dealing with timeframes. We have made recommendations to the minister in that regard.
One of the problems that I have with this bill is what I quoted back from Coulter earlier. Coulter indicated that there were special circumstances that had to be looked at, and those special circumstances were for farmers and fishermen.
Under the revindication requirement as outlined in the legislation before us in Bill C-22, one of the problems that we have is that it says the goods, in order to revindicate, must be in the same form that they were sold.
Everybody knows that when you catch a fish and you sell it to a processing plant, it has to do something with it because it will start to rot. As soon as you get it in the processing plant, you have to do something to enhance its quality or to stabilize its quality.
The bill is very clear. In order to revindicate, under the proposals, it has to have no value-add. In the case of farmers and fishermen, in perishable goods, as soon as the product arrives at the processing plant something has to be done to preserve the quality, and that is value-add.
A farmer or fishermen might sell their goods at three o'clock today. The company goes into bankruptcy or receivership at four o'clock and they will never be able to avail themselves in almost every single case, particularly

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
fish products and fungible and perishable agricultural goods.
They will never be able to use these very good revindication provisions because there would have been value-add or there would have been some altering.
One of the things that I would suggest to the minister who is listening attentively over there is that the department go ahead with the consultative process as quickly as possible to find ways to ensure that in those two special circumstances for our farmers and our fishermen we give them similar protection that we seem to be giving to producers and sellers of other products and that we recognize the unique hardship caused if the farmer sells all his grain to a grain elevator and it is dumped in with the grain of two other farmers.
If they go bankrupt he cannot get his grain back because he does not know which 20 tonnes of grain are his and which 20 tonnes are his neighbours.
I talked to the minister about this, and I hope that we can work with him to try to come up with a workable solution so that farmers and fishermen as suppliers of goods receive similar and at least as much protection as this bill would give to the producers of other types of goods.
I have got some recommendations for him and I think he has already got them on his desk.
Some of the other things that we have looked at in the bill deal with consumer bankruptcies. The bill goes a long way to addressing a very outdated process for dealing with consumer bankrupts.
It has provisions in it for reorganization. The consumers who finds themselves in a debt situation are not left for their bones to be picked by their creditors. They have an opportunity to sit down and work with their creditors in a protected environment where nobody can really take any action while they are filing a proposal or putting it together, and so they may be able to discharge the debt in a reasonable period of time.
If those individuals who have $5,000 or less in assets, the consumers, have to go bankrupt, the act provides for a less onerous process whereby they can file an application for bankruptcy. If it is their first bankruptcy, nine months later, unless there is a major objection agreed to by the courts or by the superintendent, automatically they get discharged. They are very positive and important amendments to the bill.
There are just two other things I want to talk about.
I think the minister would have to agree with me that it is simply not the case that a lot of the rhetoric is coming out from the department and from promoters of this particular bill about all of the Crown priorities that have been given up. The Crown priorities as they relate to source deductions are still firmly in place. For most medium and small sized businesses it is a fairly large chunk and it is a very heavy top priority to be given.
We have recommended in our committee report, and the Liberal party recommends it, a re-examination of that. We also recommend that the Crown be treated as any other creditor in so far as the putting together of a proposal.
The last thing that I want to say is there are a lot of regulations. We cannot keep passing laws-this is one of those pieces of legislation-and leaving the actual mechanism to enact the legislation to regulators. There are over 130 pieces of regulation that have to be written.
The Liberal Party wants to look at those in committee before we agree to anything further with the bill because we believe that passing bills has to be put back on the shoulders of parliamentarians. We should not pass shells of bills and then at that point leave it to regulators actually to put the mechanisms together that will make or break the legislation.
In conclusion, I would like to say that the Liberal Party has been supportive of any effort to reform the legislation. I have tried in the short period I have had to outline what we think is good about the legislation and what we support. I have given our support for the process under which we have embarked. I also have major difficulties and cannot reconcile my difficulties, no matter how often I have talked to the minister and his officials, with the wage earner protection fund as put forward.
October 29, 1991

The Liberal Party simply cannot accept another tax on Canadian businesses. As much as we want to support this legislation and as much as we know that there have been major reforms made, at this point I would have to move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the
word "that" and by substituting the following therefor:
"That this House declines to proceed with Bill C-22, an act to enact the Wage Claim Payment Act, to amend the Bankruptcy Act and to amend other acts in consequence thereof, the principle of which is to impose yet another tax on Canadian business".

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The Chair will take under advisement the motion in amendment proposed by the hon. member for Dartmouth.

Before recognizing the next speaker, it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Surrey North-Health; the hon. member for Restigouche- Chaleur-Canada Post; the hon. member for Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffville-Pornography; the hon. member for Mount Royal-The Economy; the hon. member for Saint-Leonard-Paper Industry.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about Bill C-22, an act to enact the Wage Claim Payment Act and to amend the Bankruptcy Act.
When we had the little 10-minute debates before we sent Bill C-22 to a pre-study committee I remember saying it was appropriate that we should amend the Bankruptcy Act. This is the first time since 1949 when the act was passed that there has been a bill to amend the act.
Colleagues of my caucus and I over several Parliaments have called for amendments to the 1949 Bankruptcy Act because it has become outdated. It does not reflect the realities of today.
In fact from 1975 to 1984 there were six bills introduced by my colleagues to the right, the Liberals. Some of them included super priority. The last Consumer and Corporate Affairs minister in the Liberal government,
Government Orders
the Trudeau government, brought in an amendment to the act and what happened? She included super priority.
Well, something happened on the way to the House of Commons after the act was introduced. Some group or somebody got to the minister and that act just died.
We have had a new government since 1984. Seven years later and four ministers later, we have C-22. Every minister who occupied the position of Consumer and Corporate Affairs minister since 1984 always said: "Oh, this is a priority for me. We have got to do something about it".
When this minister introduced his bill for first reading, I stood up here and said: "This bill that the minister introduced reminds me of a fireman going to the blazing inferno with a step ladder and a garden hose" because there were criticisms I had made of things in the bill.
' Well, we introduced a brand new process. The minister got very wise. He decided to try out a new strategy so he said: "Maybe I could suck these guys in". He came up with what is called pre-study. A nice concept. I had no problem with it. Anybody who wants to talk, why not get together. He sent the bill to pre-study and what we did in the pre-study, I am proud to say, is we gave him a fire hose and an extension ladder. I think that is what our recommendations did.
I want to point out that it is very seldom in this House that we get the kind of unanimity of thinking on major important issues as we did. There is only one recommendation in the 22 that I could not agree with. It is a minor one and not very crucial to the bill. I want to say to the minister that in fact we had Conservatives on the committee, colleagues from the Liberal Party and myself, and we came out of that process with 22 recommendations. We were unanimous in agreeing on the vast majority of them including the important ones, the wage payment protection provisions.
We were concerned about the walk-aways. We agreed on the revindication of goods. We were agreed on the breathing space for re-organization. We were in agreement on the provisions for consumer bankruptcies. We had no problem. It was marvellous. It was a real love-in because we were cheek to cheek, eyeball to eyeball, jowl to jowl on the important issues.

October 29, 1991
Government Orders
I support the process and I have no problem with it. The whole concept of the pre-study, the whole raison d'etre behind the pre-study is so that members can aerate and explore the provisions of a bill that had second reading. They can come to an agreement on very important issues, not the minor dotting of the i's and crossing of the t's and putting in the commas, but on the crucial issues, the real principle issues in the bill. If we can reach agreement on that, what is the point if the minister simply says: "Well, I don't think you have any relevancy" or "I do not agree with you on that" or "my way or the highway"?
What is the point of that? What is the point of that exercise? I want to come to the major disagreements that we had. I want the minister to know that in this examination of pre-study of this bill, we did not exactly go to the highways and by-ways and say: "You come to the committee. We want to hear your views on bankruptcy". We did not advertise in newspapers all across the country. We did not invite every Tom, Dick, Harry, Jane, Elizabeth to come and say what they want. We did not have these sorts of town hall meetings that we see now with different committees that go around the country. We did not do that.
I want to put this in context. We did not do that. I want to deal with what the minister said, that of all these witnesses who came, only one supported super priority. We decided we would call only these people who have an interest in the bill: the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and I want to ask you who they represent; the Canadian Bar Association; the Canadian Insolvency Association; the Canadian Institute of Public Real Estate Companies; Insolvency Institute of Canada; the Canadian Bankers' Association; the Board of Trade of Metropolitan Toronto; Pfeiffer & Pfeiffer, trustees and liquidators; C. Roy Henning, Barrister and Solicitor; Weir Bowen, Edmonton, Alberta and so on and so on.
The overwhelming number of the witnesses who came were agents for bankers back then and bandits. That is how it is. These are the ones we heard from. They are the ones who would come and say: "Oh, you can't give workers a super priority. You can't interfere with the secured creditors. You can't do that. You are going to have credit crunch".
You cannot deal with walk-aways they said. You cannot touch them. We listened to all of that. We listened to the concern of the Canadian Labour Congress which had always in the past supported super priority, but which were concerned that if you give workers a super priority and the operation goes bankrupt there may not be any assets. There may not be any assets from which the workers may get some money. That was the concern they had.
We listened to all of that. Then we said to them: "Be gone". We closed the doors. We had our discussions. We had long discussions and fruitful discussions, and on the major questions we chose to make recommendations to the minister. I want to pick the most important recommendation in my view. Others are important, but this I think was the most important one. It is the one that has occupied my attention since I came into the House of Commons. That was to make sure that when a company goes bankrupt the workers' wages are paid. That was my commitment.
My friend from Broadview-Greenwood knows that. I used to make these speeches. I have private members' bills. The way I see it there is a moral responsibility that goes beyond bankers and financial institutions. If there are assets then the moral responsibility is that their wages get paid first before anything else. That is imperative. From evidence that we received, in 90 per cent of the cases there are assets. When a bank makes a loan to a business you can be darned sure that it protects its bunnies by making sure that there is greater value in the assets than the amount it is lending. And so there are.
The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that we had all the people who had a vested interest in making sure that their clients did not lose their super priority in the Senate when an occupation or an operation goes bankrupt.
We are going to get to that, brother. Just cool your buns.
When you think about it, the evidence was that this amounts to about $61 million in the government's proposed wage protection plan. Think of all of the loan portfolios out there. Think of what the money is in all of that. Surely $61 million has got to be, in my quick calculation, about less than half of one per cent of the total amount out there in loan portfolios. That for me was the most important question.

October 29, 1991

The minister had proposed in his bill a wage protection plan which would be contributed to by employers only. Can you imagine a Conservative government in this climate? It has brought on the recession we are in, it has created most of the economic problems this country faces today, and in this climate it is saying to the employers after bringing in the GST: "We are going to put another tax on you".
Here we are faced with the potential of an increase in unemployment insurance premiums come January because the government opted out of that in C-21. It put all of that on to the employers and employees. To make this fund solvent, because it is $5 billion in the hole, you would have to raise premiums 14 per cent in January. Here is a government that is now coming to small and medium-sized businesses and saying to them: "You are going to pay 10 cents an employee a week". The minister says that 10 cents is buying one little peanut, it is not a lot of money. I think he made a comparison to peanuts, or something like that. He said it is not a lot of money. Mr. Speaker, that is where it all starts. It all starts very small.
Think back to what UI premiums were and look where they are today. Look at where income tax started and look at where it is today.
The small and medium-sized business community represented by the Federation of Independent Business clearly came out against that. Look at this prospect. Think about this: There are approximately 500,000 employees in the finance sector of the country. That means the financial institutions will pay approximately $3 million a year.
Mr. Speaker, look at it. Isn't that a wonderful thing? It's like paying for protection to keep your secured creditor position. They have a deal. In fact I would suggest we put in super priority and somebody with a bright idea could invite Lloyds to come in with a suitcase and a computer and offer bankruptcy insurance and make money at it.
I see my friend from Broadview-Greenwood nodding. There is an idea.
This is what we are doing. I have been getting letters from school boards and hospital associations, concerned because they are going to be covered by this. School boards in Saskatchewan have written to me and I am
Government Orders
sure other members of Parliament will start getting letters.
In the long run where do school boards and hospitals get the money to pay their employees? They get it from the homeowner.
What this government is doing is putting another tax right on top of a heavily taxed small and medium-sized sector at the moment. I cannot imagine anything more cruel.
There is another question the committee looked at when we discussed the wage protection plan. That is the walk-aways, companies that are not technically bankrupt. They have closed the door. The owners have gone fishing in the Gulf of Mexico. The workers turn up and there is nobody there and no work. We said under the government's plan: "That is not fair". It is not fair at all. Those employers would have paid on behalf of the employees into a wage protection fund, but they are not protected. It seems to me that is not ethical. The money they were led to believe was in the fund on their behalf and the plant is closed but they cannot collect their wages from the fund. We call those the walk-aways.
I want to tell the minister, we are not prepared on this side of the House to give any final approval to this bill unless the question of the walk-aways is dealt with. We in the committee looked at the question of the walkaways and made some suggestions. We felt they could be handled out of general revenues. After all, the minister has brought in the GST. It is doing very well in the very tough time of recession. He says it is holding its own.
If it is holding its own in tough recessionary times, can you imagine when things get better how much they will be rolling in the dough?
The responsibility is to look after the victims of walk-aways. We felt that was important.
We also heard: "Oh, you are going to have a credit crunch. If you put workers ahead of the secured creditors, you are going to have a credit crunch". When we dealt with the revindication, when we discussed revindication as proposed in the bill, we heard the same argument from the banks. They said: "If you let the

Government Orders
suppliers come and take their goods, 30 days from date of delivery you are going to have a credit crunch".
Quebec has had revindication of goods. The evidence we got from the province of Quebec was that it did not lead to any credit crunch. Credit in Quebec is not higher to businesses than it is in Ontario or any other part of Canada as a result of the fact that it had a revindication of goods.
For heavens sake, do not tell me that the $61 million based on a loan portfolio of billions of dollars is going to create a credit crunch. I do not believe it for one moment.
The other thing we said was that we wanted to speed up the payment to the workers. We suggested that we could move from the proposed six weeks the minister talked about in his wage protection plan to four weeks or less. We dealt with it by providing and dealing with the Canadian Labour Congress concern, the establishment of a fund by the Superintendent of Bankruptcies.
He could increase his administrative charges for bankruptcies and from that fund he could pay whatever the shortfall is in the moneys owed to workers. We increased the workers to $3,000 from $2,000 and we allowed walk-aways $1,500.
I am torn because of the fact that on the one hand I do want to see amendments to the Bankruptcy Act. I do want to see it upgraded, but I am not prepared to sacrifice the concerns of workers in a bankruptcy or in a walk-away just because I want to see some updating of the act.
I want to move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the
word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
This House declines to give second reading to Bill C-22, an act to enact the Wage Claim Payment Act, to amend the Bankruptcy Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, as the economic climate makes this an inopportune time to impose a new tax, notably on small and medium size businesses.
