That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of ending all NATO-NORAD low-level flight training in Canada, rejecting the establishment of NATO operations in Canada, including the proposed tactical fighter and weapons training centre at Goose Bay, Labrador, and redirecting Canada's NATO-NORAD funding toward enabling Canada's aboriginal people to regain control of their lands and their livelihood and promoting sustainable development for all Canadians.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very glad of the chance to speak on this motion that I have introduced. Although
Private Members' Business
the matter of the low-level flights over the aboriginal people of what we call Labrador and eastern Quebec is much in the news, the low-level flights are continuing. Even though for the time being NATO has said it does not want to establish a base there, it is clear that the Canadian government by its statements earlier this year regrets that decision and would be happy if NATO would reverse that decision.
Therefore, both in the present and as a future possible threat, this matter of the low-level flights over Nitassi-nan, which is the name given to it by the people who have lived there for 9,000 years, is a serious threat to the people over whom the flights are tested.
I want to touch on the historical background first of all. While it only concerns a few thousand people in one comer of Canada, it is an example of something that has been going on for several centuries, that is to say the wilful destruction of indigenous people by the people who have been moving out from Europe and settling places like North America. These people were not causing anyone else any harm. They have not made war on anyone. They have simply lived there for about 9,000 years, according to what we are told and they want to continue living in the land that they have occupied.
They have lived there by sharing the land. They do not put fences around a plot and say: "You can't walk on here unless you pay me rent". They share the land they believe was created by the Creator to be used by all people with reasonable sharing and that includes the people who are yet unborn, the future generations. The land should not be damaged so that they cannot use it.
In their way of life, they live by co-operation. The children, parents and the elders live together in their settlements and moved as was necessary because of the limitations of the food in any one area. They maintained for dozens of generations a society of mutual respect.
I do not mean that nothing ever went wrong in there, but society was based on an assumption of mutual respect so that problems that did arise could be dealt with, with co-operation. This shows even in the present time, because it is a little less than half a century since most of these people were brought into the style of life that was imported into that land and other parts of North America by the immigrants from Europe, the ancestors of so many of us.

Private Members' Business
When these people are able to live on the land in their own way, their family life, their social life is much healthier. It is when they accept being drawn into makeshift housing settlements around places like Goose Bay that many of them fall into difficulties and addictions and bad habits which they have a difficult time to control.
They are not the only ones in our settlements who have these bad habits, but they show particular vulnerability to them except when they are able to go back for half the year at a time and live on the land which is where their social organization, their moral tradition is founded.
For the last four decades we have increasingly prevented them from doing this. We took a chunk of their land because we found there was a rich iron mine. They were simply pushed out of that. They were not allowed to hunt there to the extent that the hunting interfered with the iron mine operations and the transportation to and from the iron mine and the city that grew up there.
Then we found the opportunity to create a great hydro dam on the Churchill River. We flooded a section of the Churchill River. We covered not only their hunting grounds but the grounds where their ancestors were buried, a number of them. Without any notice the waters began to rise and they had to get out, taking what belongings they could take with them in a huny.
They were given no compensation for it. We simply took their land by an act of violence, even though it may not have involved any physical fighting between any of us and any of them.
Then in the more recent decades we have again taken their land and large chunks of their land for low-level flight training, training of NATO flight pilots for wars somewhere else but having an immediate destructive effect on the people who lived there for 9,000 years and in fact, according to all reports, having the effect over a number of years of endangering the very existence of that society and even within that, then, the physical, social and moral well-being of the individual people.
This present low-level flight training means that pilots are trained to fly about 30 metres above the ground over the hills, up and down, and especially along the river valleys.
The argument is that by doing this, when they are attacking places like eastern Europe they can fly underneath the radar undetected in order to bomb or strafe
enemy targets in the rear of the enemy's supposedly advancing armies.
Great Britain, Germany and Netherlands at present continue this low-level flight training. Italy may be joining them. The United States, for reasons of expense, has temporarily pulled out, but earlier this year the government predicted that there would be 7,000 or 8,000 flights per year over these zones of the inner land in order to train these people for attack.
The Department of National Defence announced that it would hope it would actually rise to more than 18,000.1 do not know yet actually how many there have been this year or will be although the season is nearly ended.
The inner people are being harassed, terrified and damaged by these low-level flights. When you are out in a canoe with your family fishing or whatever else is to be done in a canoe and the plane comes over you at 30 metres, it is terrifying. There is the startle effect. There is the general stress effect of extremely loud noise and there is the uneasiness afterwards wondering when those planes will come back.
Children have been known to jump out of the canoe into the water in their terror and some of the children now do not wish to go with their parents any more to the land because of the terrifying effect of the fighter airplanes. It is not only low-level flying. It is also bombing practice. They do not, as far as I understand, actually use live bombs but they set up targets and identify them photographically by the simulating attacks of the airplanes. There are 57 of these bombing targets unidentified on Innu land and they are planning to build another such area northwest of Goose Bay for bombing targets.
This Innu land that is being used for targets also extends into eastern Quebec, in fact about 50 per cent of the low-level flight area is in Quebec around the towns of Natashquan and La Romaine. The Innu people there have suffered very heavily as have the Innu people living in Labrador.
There have been environmental studies. The environmental assessment panel is still studying it. I do not know how long it will take to study it. They want to revise their study because of the present removal of the plans for a NATO base, but according to the Innu people most of the faults of the plan identified within the study are still there, that is 36 out of the 38 deficiencies in which they

are deficient from standards set by the environmental assessment panel.
The Innu people in Labrador have agreed to enter preliminary discussions about land claims which were long delayed by the government. They were put way down the list for land claims while the destruction of their land continues. They are willing to enter preliminary discussions with the governments of Canada and Newfoundland. They hope that maybe in a year and a half they will be able to define the scope of the negotiations for land claims and find out whether there will be some interim protection measures rather than chasing the people out of the land while we have a long-winded debate about whose land it is and what claims those people have there.
It is like the principle of being innocent until you are proved guilty. You should not be driven out of your land while it is being decided whether that is your land when you have been living there for 9,000 years.
The government claims it is uninhabited. What it means is that these people do not have a piece of paper saying: "This is a title deed and I own this land", but they have occupied that land for 9,000 years.
In Quebec the land claim discussions are going ahead under Le Conseil attikamek-montagnais that represents the Innu people there under that name.
As I said these noise levels from the flights have been identified as being very harmful primarily to the people but also to the caribou which is a major source of food in the half-year when they live on that land, to migratory waterfowl and birds of prey, also sources of food, and partly because the exhaust of the airplanes and the fuel that they sometimes dump into the rivers or lakes contaminate the waterways and contaminate the moss that the caribou eat.
The Department of National Defence has claimed that they have an avoidance strategy of staying five kilometres away from any concentration of caribou or waterfowl. What the Innu claim is that in too many of the sensitive areas it is not possible because the Innu and the caribou or the waterfowl that they hunt tend to use the waterways, the rivers and lakes, and that is what the low-level flights use. They follow the valleys. That is the whole point: flying low in the valley to keep underneath and out of detection of the radar.
Private Members' Business
They both want the same areas and it has not been possible in fact for the low-level flights to avoid them. In spite of the stated policy the low-level flights, for example, continue at Shipiskan Lake and at Wuchusk Lake. The DND finds out where they are because when they fly in there in the spring the bush pilots know where they deposited them. The DND have them registered there in their published memos known as Goose Bay Operation Directives. These two lakes, Shipiskan and Wuchusk, were both listed on the operations directive for May 31, 1991, but they still receive frequent overflights. It has been going on all summer. DND is not serious in claiming that it tries to avoid these people. It just does not avoid them. It knows they are there and still overflies them.
The Innu have done everything they can to make their point. They have spoken to the government for years. They pointed out that they were never conquered, never ceded their land. All they want is to be allowed to live in peace, which they did before we came.
They have complained to Ottawa. They have been put off with discussions of land claims some time in the future, while the flights go on. They have won support from a good deal of the public and the churches in Canada, but also in the United States, in Britain, in The Netherlands and in Germany because these people know what the low-level flights are like. They demanded that the low-level flights be eliminated or at least greatly reduced in those countries, and so they understand what the people in Labrador and eastern Quebec are suffering.
What is at stake here is not only the appeal of the present generation, but a deeper principle. These people are have respected the ancient tradition of maintenance of the land for themselves, their neighbours and future generations. Right now they have been willing to defend the land.
When I visited there two years ago one lady told me that on her grandfather's deathbed he said: "If the white people come, don't bother them; but if they hurt the land, defend it". She did, with others, defend it non-violently. She and others walked on to the airstrip and dared the planes to land while about a hundred or so of them were sitting there. Families went, mothers, fathers,

October 29, 1991
Private Members' Business
children and the elders walking with canes, and sat down on the airstrip.
They knew they faced courts, they knew they faced prisons, but they had to make their point to defend their land in the only way they could. The system of land sharing, which is many thousands of years old in all parts of the world, has now come face to face with the very recent invention of private property of the land and all the wars that go with private property in the land, and with the most mighty war machine in the world, the NATO air force along with its army.
There is no justification for continuing this. Nobody thinks Russia is going to invade Canada or western Europe. The whole rationale that was put forward for this has totally collapsed over the past couple of years. But the low-level flights continue.
In fact, low-level training has never been used in eastern Europe but it has been used in the Middle East, in the gulf war against the people of Iraq, where there was little or no danger of their being detected by radar. In other words, this technique is continuing to be used, people are trained to use it, not so as to defend Canada or western Europe from invasion by the Soviet Union but to be used when we, as extensions of the west European nations, intend to invade other lands, whether it is to take the oil of the Middle East or something else, whether it be in South America, in Africa or in parts of Asia.
In order to be prepared to destroy other indigenous people, we are now year by year destroying the indigenous people of parts of northeastern Quebec and of Labrador. It is a shame that the Canadian government continues to do this, either for profit or for the sake of imperial conquest in the southern parts of this globe.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina.
There has been an air base at Goose Bay since 1942. There was no community there before that so the air base is the community.
Of course the mission since the 1960s has been low-level flying. This practice is carried on over the Ungava Peninsula because the terrain is similar to that to be overflown in eastern Europe and because of the
density of the population in western Europe, particularly West Germany. What is practised is flying at low altitude so as to avoid enemy radar.
There are those who say the mission should not be carried on because, first, it is offensive not defensive.
The Follow on Forces strategy is designed to penetrate deep into enemy territory, but only following an enemy first strike. The policy of NATO is still no first strike. However, once attacked the policy of NATO for Follow on Forces is to penetrate enemy territory so as to attack installations behind the front line and to disrupt supply lines. In that context it is a defence measure.
Second, it sends the wrong signal and we should discontinue low-level flying as a Canadian contribution to NATO.
We are a partner in NATO. The low-level flying is part of our contribution to NATO. It should only be discontinued as part of a NATO strategy and after consultation among NATO partners.
Peace is breaking out rapidly. But because we were strong not because we were weak. A time of rapid change is not time to make change in defence posture unilaterally, rather reduction of forces should be balanced. It may be that in the course of disarmament discussions the Follow on Forces attack policy of NATO will be discontinued and low-level flying deemed unnecessary. That is a decision for NATO.
Third, the Innu consider Labrador their homeland and the low-level flying a threat to their culture and environment.
The Innu are the original people of Labrador. There is no question that the Innu society today is fragile or that the Innu, a minority in Ungava, feel threatened by the society of the majority all around them, or that there are other serious problems in their communities, such as alcohol, abuse, social decay.
But others consider it their homeland too-the Inuit, the Metis, the Newfoundlanders, those from other parts of Canada, including Quebec. People from all these latter groups work at Goose Bay. Some are second and third generation residents. If the base were to close, the jobs, homes, schools, businesses that these people have built and are building would disappear, all in a province which has the highest unemployment rate in Canada, and the lowest per capita income, where the main
October 29, 1991

industry, the fishery industry, is in crisis, and where there are no obvious alternatives.
The Innu have rights. The others who live in Labrador have rights too. How are the rights of all the people of Labrador to be addressed? Or what must be done to ensure that all the people of Labrador live in harmony and that some do not threaten or displace others.
A process is in motion that will shed light on the problem. FEARO, the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office, has received the environmental impact statement regarding low-level flying and the NATO base and will be holding public hearings this winter.
My position is that we should wait for the report of the FEARO panel before deciding for or against low-level flying, for or against the NATO Tactical Training Centre, which NATO cancelled its plans announced May 22,
1990.	Beyond that, the situation remains basically the same particularly with respect to the importance of the military to the well-being of the community.
I hope an accommodation can be found that will allow all of the people of Labrador to live in harmony. The first step in the right direction is an immediate start and a speedy conclusion to the settlement of Innu land claims. Within this land claims process provision must be made for the tailoring of military activities to fit the livelihoods of local people.
I hope and I believe this is possible.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina has put forward three proposals. The first that the government should consider the advisability of ending NATO and NORAD low-level training in Canada. Second, we should reject the establishment of NATO operations in Canada including the training centre that was at one time proposed for Goose Bay. Third, we should direct the funds now spent on NATO and NORAD toward enabling Canada's aboriginal people to regain control of their lands and their livelihood in promoting sustainable development for all Canadians.
The wording of the motion suggests that the hon. member does not fully understand the reason for low-level flying in Canada and does not understand all the social and economic impacts of what he really is propos-
Private Members' Business
ing. The lack of understanding is not surprising since there is a lot of misinformation out there concerning low-level flying in general and about Goose Bay in particular.
I am afraid that many well meaning Canadians share the hon. member's confusion. I welcome this opportunity to try to clarify some of the issues.
Let me begin by explaining just how much low-level training is really being conducted here in Canada. On the NORAD side no routine low-level flying is conducted by NORAD assigned aircraft except in designated areas associated with our flying training schools, such as the one at Cold Lake in Alberta.
However, the United States Strategic Air Command does from time to time conduct low-level navigation training along authorized routes within Canada. On occasion Canadian NORAD assigned fighter aircraft conduct practice interceptions of these aircraft and may for brief periods operate at low altitudes.
I do not believe however that these are the flights that are causing concern for the hon. member. Strictly speaking, no NATO low-level flying is conducted in Canada either. However, three NATO nations are entitled to conduct low-level training out of Goose Bay, Labrador, under the terms of bilateral agreements with Canada. This training is frequently referred to as NATO training.
I have no objection to that terminology except to note that it is strictly not accurate. At one time Goose Bay was being considered by NATO as a site for a new tactical fighter centre. In early 1990 NATO abandoned the proposal to establish that centre. The tactical fighter and weapons training centre referred to in the motion is therefore essentially a dead issue.
Any comments that I shall make about Goose Bay today will apply to our existing bilateral agreements, not to the NATO centre mentioned in the motion.
To understand the significance of what the hon. member is proposing, one has to understand why low-level flying is necessary. Many people I regret to say have been led to believe that allied pilots operate at low-level altitudes solely as means of flying undetected over eastern European countries en route to launch a surprise attack. That idea of course is ludicrous, but it is actively promoted by various groups, groups who are opposed to

October 29, 1991
Private Members' Business
Canada's involvement in NATO and who do not let the truth interfere with their anti-military agendas.
In fact, low-level flying is a vital part of virtually all tactical fighter operations. Modem air defence weapons are so accurate and so fast in reacting that the life expectancy of a pilot operating in altitude of much more than 30 metres in hostile airspace would be measured in minutes, if not in seconds.
Fighter aircraft must operate over hostile territory if they are to be of any use. If allied nations should ever become involved in a war, fighter aircraft would be a key factor in protecting friendly troops and preventing enemy forces from sustaining an advance.
Many of their missions would be flown at low altitudes over enemy held territory, relatively close to the front lines. Therefore, it is essential that fighter pilots feel as much at home at 30 metres as they do at 300 metres and that takes a great deal of training and a great deal of practice.
I am told that high speed low-level flying is perhaps the most challenging role that any pilot will ever face and that those who lack proficiency become a menace to themselves and to others.
Canadian and other allied pilots should not be expected to risk their lives on our behalf unless they have been given the best training available and that includes low-level flying.
To suggest that low-level flying is a needless frill or worse, that it is an aggressive tactic associated solely with a first strike strategy, is both inaccurate and irresponsible. The question is not whether low-level flying training is necessary, but rather where it should be done.
The hon. member for Trinity-Spadina has suggested that it should not be allowed in Canada. Presumably he wonders why our allies do not train in their own countries. They do train in their own countries to the best extent possible.
Each year about 80,000 low-level training flights are conducted in the United Kingdom alone. That is about 10 times as many flights as are conducted out of Goose Bay by all the allied participants combined.
However, there are problems with low-level flying in Europe. This kind of training is difficult. It is difficult because the countries are small and densely populated and the landscape is dotted with towns, power lines, hospitals, airports and other obstacles to low flying aircraft. Many restrictions are, therefore, necessary on both the routing and the altitude within Europe.
In Canada, on the other hand, we can designate low level training in areas that have none of these obstacles. We can offer a resource to our allies that is unobtainable elsewhere, and that resource is space.
To deny our allies the use of that resource for a relatively modest low flying program that lasts only eight months of each year would call into question Canada's commitment to the allegiance.
There is no free ride. If Canada is going to derive the benefits of collective security and if we are going to use European air space for our own training programs as we have done for years, then we must be prepared to make a contribution in return. The provision of low level training areas is only one way in which we can make an immensely important contribution to the alliance at very little cost.
It is no secret that the New Democratic Party has long opposed our membership in NATO and has long objected to our contributions to the alliance. Few members of this House will therefore be surprised that the motion now before us calls for an end to both our financial contributions and our provisions of air space for low-level flying.
I would like to go on record today as saying categorically that this Government of Canada does not subscribe to those isolationist views. We regard NATO as one of the cornerstones of our foreign and defence policy and will continue to support it politically, militarily and financially as long as the need exists.
That is not to say that we believe in business as usual. Far from it. With the changes that are now taking place in eastern Europe, the role of NATO will certainly change. We will see, for example, a grater emphasis on the political component of the alliance and less on the military component.
We will see a diminishing reliance on nuclear weapons, but the value of NATO as a force for stability and international co-operation will most definitely continue.
October 29, 1991

In the months and in the years to come we can expect to see NATO play a larger role in the disarmament efforts in establishing contacts with the countries of eastern Europe. As a matter of fact, Canadians can hold their heads high in Europe because they have always done their share.
I believe Canadians want to continue to do their share to reaffirm and reconfirm their commitment to collective defence. I believe that Canadians would want us to defeat the motion now before us and I propose that we do just that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Trinity-Spadi-na for presenting this motion.
I am not sure it is going to be voted on, but in any case I am sure if there were a vote we would find the Liberals and Conservatives again voting on the same side. They almost read off the same speech notes. I would not be surprised about that either.
The Conservative member was so eloquent about low-level flying I thought for a moment she was going to recommend that it be done over southern Calgary.
I understand from the member's interjection that she is saying it should be done over northern Alberta.
It is interesting that low-level flying is okay to that member, provided it is done over land that she considers empty land. What I am suggesting is that is one of the problems in Canada. Nobody is talking here about our commitment to NATO or to NORAD or to good training for our military personnel.
We would all like to see our military personnel flying under the safest possible conditions. What we are talking about here is a concept that is of concern and is disturbing to many Canadians. That is the idea that land occupied now and for the last 9,000 years by aboriginal people is considered empty land.
That is an attitude which suggests that aboriginal people in this country are non-persons, and that is the concern that I have.
The member talked about our commitment to the alliance. I think everybody in this world recognizes that Canada has made a commitment to NATO, is a member of NATO and exercises its commitment and lives up to its commitment.
Private Members' Business
What is this alliance set up to serve? My understanding was that the alliance was established at the time of the last war to defend the democratic states of Europe and North America, and to make sure that those nations on the other side which did not defend the rights of individuals and the rights of human beings would end up not being triumphant in that war. That is why NATO was put together.
It seems to me that this low-level flying base violates the principles upon which NATO was originally established, because if what we are saying by continuing low-level flying over aboriginal territory is that they have to sacrifice their rights, their subsistence and that their lives, their futures and their land are of no consequence at all when measured against our commitment to the alliance, then that alliance no longer is based on the principles upon which it was established in the first place.
I think that is the issue that Canada should be re-examining when it looks at what it is doing to the Inuit people in northern Labrador and Quebec.
The Prime Minister in the last little while has been travelling to Commonwealth conferences and cabinet ministers have been travelling to China for example suggesting that in the future Canadian foreign aid is going to be tied to human rights performance on the part of the recipients of Canadian aid.
I think in cases such as this we should be examining exactly what Canada's human rights performance is and how we treat our aboriginal people. Canada's image is examined around the world and the image that many people have of Canada and its human rights record was formed at the time of the Oka dispute last summer when they saw the Canadian Armed Forces of 2,000 people lined up against 55 Mohawks who were attempting to defend their land and the rights to their land within the province of Quebec.
That is the image that many people around the world have of Canada and its performance with respect to human rights. The image that many other people have across the world when they hear Canada talking about human rights is the image of an aboriginal Innu woman being dragged off a runway in northern Labrador and dragged into court because she had the temerity to try to defend her land and her subsistence against the multimillion of dollars that were being spent to establish a low-level flying training base in Labrador.

Private Members' Business
The image that many people have of Canada and its human rights performance around the world is the image of Innu and aboriginal communities in northern Canada where there are no flush toilets, where there is no running water, where there is no adequate school system, where there is no adequate health care services, where families have disintegrated as a result of the way that Canada has treated those families and isolated them on the margins of Canadian society. That is the image many people have of Canada's human rights performance that the Prime Minister is trying to defend at Commonwealth conferences and in the meetings of NATO.
I suggest that the issue we are debating today is an issue of Canada's human rights performance. What the member opposite was saying was that the government considers land occupied by the Innu now and from time immemorial to be empty land. I say that is part of the problem we are experiencing in this country. This government considers northern aboriginal people as nonpeople. That is the issue we are dealing with here.
Nobody is suggesting that there should not be low-level flights. That is a red herring. Nobody is suggesting that our pilots and the personnel in the armed forces of Canada and other members of the alliance should not have the kind of training they need in order for them to be safe and effective. That is not the issue here. That is not what we are talking about.
What we are talking about is the fact that Canada has selected from among all of the areas in Canada land occupied by aboriginal people in order to do this low-level flying. It has said said that the subsistence, the hunting and fishing that these people do is secondary. It has said that these people are second-class citizens in terms of their right to hunt and fish free of the interference of foreign and Canadian military fighters doing their low-level training over the area, because it has never been questioned that this kind of flying has interfered with the subsistence activities of the Innu people and deprived them of the right to hunt and fish with some security. Nobody has ever suggested that.
The problem here is not as the member for Calgary suggests, that the NDP is opposed to Canada's participation in NATO. The problem is not that we would like to see our fighters go without low-level flying training. The
problem here is that Canada does not respect the very human rights that it commands other countries in the world to respect as a condition of receiving foreign aid from us.
I would hope that the member from Calgary would reconsider the statement she made. I would hope that the Liberals would reconsider the position they have taken on the Goose Bay, Labrador site and the low-level flying training that takes place in northern Labrador and Quebec. This training is destroying the livelihood of Innu people. It is destroying the way of life of those Innu people. It is being done without their consent. It is being done in violation of their human rights. It goes against the principles that all Canadians claim to stand for. It goes against the principles that the Prime Minister trumpets Canadians stand for around the world. We should all in this House reconsider that base in northern Labrador and we should do away with that base.
On the other hand, nobody is suggesting, as the Liberal member suggested, that if we shut down the base we should do away with schools and hospitals and community services in that area, because this party has always suggested that there be a conversion strategy. That conversion strategy would plan a peaceful transition from a base in northern Labrador that is based on flying training for the purposes of war and destruction, to an economy that is based on peaceful uses. I suggest that one way we might do that is to develop through negotiations with the Innu people and through a land claims and a resource settlement the kind of economic development which would incorporate not simply the non-Innu people who live in that area, but the Innu and the non-Innu people so that jobs could be created, resource development could be embarked upon and we would not require that military base in order to maintain jobs, community infrastructure, health, education and social services facilities. That is what we should be looking at. It is unfortunate that the member for Calgary and the Liberal member who spoke did not direct themselves to those kinds of solutions, rather than simply adopting the solutions that look to the past.

Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to be part of this debate today. There has been much discussion in a pretty general way about this low-level flying program. In the next few minutes I would like to go into more detail
October 29, 1991

about the program and its economic impact on the local community.
Both those topics have a bearing on the third part of the motion now before the House, that money be diverted from NATO and NORAD to support aboriginal people and sustainable development. In a typical year our allies who participate in the Goose Bay program- Great Britain, Germany and Netherlands-arrive at Goose Bay in March or April, leave in October or November, and fly about 8,000 low-level sorties while they are there. Lest I be accused of using military jargon, I should perhaps explain that a sortie consists of a take-off and a landing.
If we were to compare the total military activity rate at Goose Bay with the rates experiences at civilian airports in the country, we would see that it is about half that of Lethbridge, Alberta, about one-seventh that of Ottawa or about one-fourteenth that of Toronto. The low-level flying itself takes place in two specially-

Mr. Speaker, the low-level flying itself takes place in two specially designated areas that together total about 100,000 square kilometres. That is an area 17 times the size of Prince Edward Island or almost twice the size of Nova Scotia. In comparison with Europe, it is about 40
Private Members' Business
per cent larger than Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg combined. Within that vast area of Canada there is not a single permanent resident. The day-to-day population density in other words is zero.
Compare that with a population density of about 300 persons per square kilometre in northwest Europe and we can immediately appreciate why the Goose Bay area is so well suited to low flying operations. If the entire population of Canada were to be moved into the Goose Bay low flying area, the resulting density would still be lower than that of the Netherlands.
It is true that hunting and fishing parties occasionally enter the flying areas for periods of up to a few weeks at a time. At the peak of the season these transient groups may increase the population density to about one person for every 100 square kilometres. Although that density is still extremely low, the equivalent of about two bus loads of people in the province of Prince Edward Island, we recognize that no one likes to be overflown by low flying aircraft. The military, therefore, have avoided low overflying areas where any persons are present and continues to offer to avoid low overflying any person or group whose position is made known to them. If a group already in the area should decide to change its movement plans, the military is willing to change its flight routes daily if necessary to accommodate them. Since most groups are in radio contact with the outside world the passing of revised travel plans should not be a problem. Overflights in the Goose Bay area are a problem only for those who wish to make them so.
By contrast, the Goose Bay low flying program brings major benefits to the community of Happy Valley, Goose Bay. During the flying season the base employs approximately 900 civilians, about one-third of whom are aboriginals, and generates an additional 1,000 to 1,200 indirect jobs. In total the base is responsible for about half the employment in the local area. In 1991 alone the base will contribute over $100 million to the Labrador economy through wages and local purchases.
We are looking here at what is essentially a one-industry town. The base exists solely to support the low flying program. If that program were to be terminated, as my hon. friend has suggested, all those jobs and all those

October 29, 1991
Private Members' Business
expenditures would cease almost immediately. We would see a thriving economy destroyed virtually overnight.
I wonder whether the member for Trinity-Spadina is aware of that. I wonder whether his party, which professes to have so much concern for the average Canadian, is aware that its doctrinaire, anti-military agenda for the Goose Bay region could force hundreds of people out of work and on to the welfare rolls.
Perhaps the hon. member feels that other industries could be attracted to the Goose Bay area to compensate for the loss of the base. If he has any ideas, I know that the people of Happy Valley, Goose Bay would be pleased to hear them. They have tried over the years to develop other industries in Labrador but none has produced more than a few scattered jobs and only a few have been economically viable.
The fact is that it is not easy to replace a $100 million a year industry in a relatively isolated part of the country. In case my hon. friend is thinking that we could merely the divert the money that is now spent on the flying program to some pie in the sky make work project or to increased welfare payments, let me set the record straight on that idea too. Most of the money being spent in Goose Bay comes not from Canada but from the European user nations. If the low flying stops the funding stops with it.
I am not suggesting that everything about the low flying program in Goose Bay is problem-free and heartily endorsed by all local residents. Problems do exist and some local residents, particularly those in the nearby aboriginal community, object strenuously to the program. But we believe that the problems can be overcome if all interested parties would work together to find solutions.
In the past five years DND has spent almost $7 million on various environmental studies to ensure that the low flying program is environmentally acceptable. In addition, the government has provided more than $2 million to the association that represents the local aboriginal communities so that they may prepare land claim documentation. A further $1 million is being spent each year by the user nations for monitoring and mitigation projects aimed at reducing or eliminating environmental problems.
The government is doing everything reasonably possible to make the Goose Bay project environmentally and socially acceptable to everyone.
No, the Goose Bay project is not without its opponents, but then how many $100 million a year industries are. In my view the benefits of the low flying program to the community of Happy Valley, Goose Bay, to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, and to the aboriginal people who wish to take advantage of it far outweigh the real or imagined disadvantages.
That notwithstanding, if it can ever be shown that the environmental problems outweigh the economic, social and military benefits, we are prepared to terminate the program at the earliest possible opportunity.
Let me move now to the final proposal embodied in the motion now before us which calls for a redirection of NATO and NORAD funding to aboriginal programs and the promotion of sustainable development.
I find this part of the motion particularly intriguing. Does the hon. member really believe that support for aboriginal peoples and for sustainable development should depend on cancellation of programs that have been a cornerstone of Canadian foreign and defence policies for decades? Is he really serious in that proposal? I suggest not.
I suggest that the motion is nothing more than a blatant attempt to curry favour with aboriginal peoples and the unemployed in the full knowledge that the underlying proposal could never be accepted. It is grandstanding.
Of course the Government of Canada will provide funding for aboriginal development. We already devote billions of dollars every year to various aboriginal programs including those associated with land claims and we are opening up new avenues every year.
Of course, sustainable development remains an objective of the Government of Canada. Why should the fate of those very worth-while programs hinge upon our withdrawal from NATO and NORAD? Where is the connection? There is none, except in the minds of the members opposite.
To conclude, let me review very briefly just what we are being asked to support. First, we are asked to deny our allies the right to use Canadian air space for training that is an essential part of military preparedness and that cannot reasonably be accomplished elsewhere. If we do

October 29, 1991
that, we will show ourselves to be an unreliable ally and will lose much of the respect we now enjoy in the alliance. At the same time, we will cause mass unemployment and hardship in an area of the country that has few, if any, employment options. The proposal is foolish in the extreme.
Second, we are asked to reject the establishment of NATO operations in Canada, including the proposed NATO tactical fighting centre. The NATO tactical fighting centre is the only NATO operation that has been considered for Canada and even that has been a dead issue for months. It is hard to understand why the hon. member is still concerned about it. If some other NATO facility were to be proposed for Canada, I suggest that the only reasonable response would be to examine it on its own merits. To ban all future NATO operations in Canada, even though none have been proposed, would needlessly call into question our commitment to the alliance. The proposal is pointless and potentially damaging.
Finally, as I have discussed, we are asked to terminate all NATO and NORAD funding so that we may divert the money to aboriginal and developmental projects. How very short-sighted that would be. Membership in NATO and NORAD provides Canada with influence in Washington and European capitals that we would otherwise lack. It enables us to advance our views about disarmament and international co-operation. It keeps us in the forefront of developments in eastern Europe and it enables us to maintain surveillance of our coast lines and to participate in other aspects of North American defence at minimum cost.
We are not so desperate that we must terminate our membership in very important international organizations so that we may further fund domestic programs, no matter how worth while they may be. The proposal, as I have already suggested, is probably nothing more than window-dressing for the NDP political agenda.
In short, the motion now before the House has nothing to recommend it. Its approval would do immeasurable harm to our international relations and our defence posture and would effectively kill a small town in one of the less advantaged parts of this country.
Private Members' Business
I invite all members of the House to join me in expressing their total rejection of an ill-conceived motion.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to today's debate on low-level flights near Goose Bay as part of Canada's commitment to NATO. I think that we must understand NATO's role in the world.
I have often heard members from the New Democratic Party say that Canada should withdraw from NATO because we have nothing to gain by remaining in that organization.
Mr. Speaker, one must remember that NATO is crucial to stability in the new Europe. This is not a new organization. It brings together politicians; it is a political group of 16 democratic countries. These are not totalitarian countries; they are not countries that do not believe in democracy; they are democratic countries.
I sincerely believe that we, as North Americans, must also give our support to these people. I was listening earlier to the member who presented the motion.
